EUobserver https://euobserver.com Independent EU journalism Tue, 10 Nov 2026 20:22:52 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.3 EU‑UK carbon market deal close, with UK courting access to ‘Made in Europe’ before Dublin summit https://euobserver.com/248253/euuk-carbon-market-deal-close-with-uk-courting-access-to-made-in-europe-before-dublin-summit/ Wed, 11 Nov 2026 06:27:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=248253 A deal between the EU and UK on carbon emissions trading and carbon tax is imminent as British ministers push for sectoral agreements ahead of next week's EU-UK summit.]]> UK and EU officials are on the brink of an agreement that would link their carbon emissions markets, a move that would save companies millions of euros in carbon border taxes, as the diplomatic push for deeper EU-UK integration accelerates ahead of a key post-Brexit summit next week. 

The deal would enable carbon permits to be traded across the two emissions systems. The UK’s post-Brexit emissions trading scheme was modelled on the EU’s. 

The UK’s carbon border adjustment mechanism, which is set to come into force early next year, is also based on the EU’s carbon border levy, a tax on imported industrial goods which are linked to high carbon emissions. 

Once the UK and EU emissions trading systems are linked, that would pave the way for them to be exempted from their respective CBAM laws.  

On Tuesday (10 November), UK trade minister Jonathan Reynolds and Europe minister Hamish Falconer held talks with EU trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič to push for a UK inclusion in the EU’s ‘Made in Europe’ initiative, that would allow UK firms to retain access to the EU’s industrial supply chain. 

Meetings with vice-president Stéphane Séjourne and defence commissioner Andrius Kubilius were also on the agenda.

]]> Best way to halt migration is to sabotage Europe’s economy – but nobody wants that, so what are the alternatives? https://euobserver.com/248074/best-way-to-stop-migration-is-to-destroy-europes-economy/ Tue, 10 Nov 2026 19:00:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=248074 Keeping people impoverished abroad and destroying its economy are Europe's best tools to stop migration. Not even the most anti-migrant politician would seriously push for such a proposal.]]> European policy and law makers have a dilemma. They want to stop irregular migration and deport as many as people as possible.

But people arriving in Europe irregularly are also lured by work. Spain needs people to pick vegetables and fruit. So does Italy.

I remember meeting a young man from Bangladesh on the Ocean Viking, freshly rescued after a harrowing night at sea, asking when he would start working in Italy.

Hein de Haas, a sociologist and university professor in Amsterdam and Maastricht, argues that European labour demand is the ultimate migration driver.

“By far the best way to stop migration is to destroy your economy,” he recently told Deutsche Welle, a German broadcaster.

Not even the most anti-migrant politician would seriously push for such a proposal.

They are instead shoring up controls and restrictions. Some are more obvious than others.

Bangladesh seems to be a pretty good example. Let me explain.

]]> Watchdog finds patchy customs controls leave big loopholes in EU’s Russia trade sanctions https://euobserver.com/248251/watchdog-finds-patchy-customs-controls-leave-big-loopholes-in-eu-russia-trade-sanctions/ Tue, 10 Nov 2026 17:27:30 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=248251 Watchdog finds spotty oversight and unclear rules weaken EU trade sanctions with Russia. Calls on customs authorities and the European Commission to do a better job.]]> When Moscow launched its war against Ukraine in early the 2022, the EU quickly announced sanctions to cripple Russia’s economy.

Twenty-one sanction packages have since been imposed, designed to punish Russia for its war. In 2021, EU trade with Russia stood at €253bn. Last year, it was €58bn.

Yet despite EU restrictions, sanctioned trade goods, both imports and exports, still manage to slip into Russia as member states grapple with weak monitoring, spotty enforcement and legal ambiguities.

This includes everything from dual-use and advanced-technology items found in Russian weapons to industrial goods vital for Russia’s economic and industrial base.

Of some 202 identified parts in Russian missiles and drones, eight came directly from the EU. Even mundane products like Birch plywood from Russia and Belarus, which get relabelled in a foreign state, end up in the EU market.

Read more

In theory it’s from China, in reality it’s from Moscow – how sanctioned Russian timber keeps flowing into Czech Republic

The findings were part of a larger report on EU sanctions on Russia, by the Luxembourg-based EU watchdog, the European Court of Auditors.

The court looked at Bulgaria, Germany, Latvia, the Netherlands, and Poland. The differences between the five, in terms of compliance, appears striking.

The report found Bulgaria recorded no violations of the sanctions. Latvia recorded 2,100. Both share borders with non-EU countries.

]]> [Interview] From aid donor to ‘geopolitical actor’: EU’s Africa diplomat on upgrading security cooperation https://euobserver.com/248162/interview-from-aid-donor-to-geopolitical-actor-eus-africa-diplomat-on-upgrading-security-cooperation/ Tue, 10 Nov 2026 16:58:09 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=248162 The EU is advancing its role as a 'geopolitical actor' by accelerating defence and security talks with a series of African states. EUobserver talks to Patricia Llombart Cussac, the managing director for Africa for the European External Action Service, the EU’s diplomatic corps.]]> “Security in Africa and security in Europe are very much linked. I think we cannot look at the world as we used to look at some few years ago,” says Patricia Llombart Cussac, the managing director for Africa for the European External Action Service, the EU’s diplomatic corps.

That’s a rebuke to those who think of ‘Fortress Europe’ and would prefer to think of the conflicts in the Horn of Africa and the Middle East as wars in far-flung regions that are of no interest to Europe.

“This is a completely different vision from the European Union as a donor. This is the European Union as a geopolitical actor. And this is what the relationship we want to continue building with the countries,” she adds.

Llombart Cussac, a former EU ambassador to Morocco, is hosting a three-day gathering of the EU’s 46 ambassadors across sub-Saharan Africa in Nairobi that started on Tuesday (10 November), where the aim was to reflect on how to strengthen what EU officials call the ‘strategic partnership’ between the bloc and Africa.

Defence and security partnerships were top of the agenda as well as the bloc’s Global Gateway investment progamme.

Read more

EU governments back Global Gateway — but insist Brussels explain where the billions go

Picking Nairobi was no coincidence, says Llombart Cussac. Kenya is one of the EU’s closest partners in Africa and is a regional hub for east Africa, and also the EU’s diplomatic operations in the region.

Dynamic cooperation

Kenya also had a formal defence and security dialogue with the EU earlier in November. Throughout 2026, the EU and Kenya are celebrating the 50 years anniversary of diplomatic relations.

Security cooperation with Kenya is “a dynamic area of our cooperation,” adds EU ambassador to Kenya, Andreas Peschke.

]]> ‘Made in Europe’ and low-carbon rules up for debate as EU eyes industrial law deal  https://euobserver.com/248217/made-in-europe-and-low-carbon-rules-up-for-debate-as-eu-eyes-industrial-law-deal/ Tue, 10 Nov 2026 16:31:48 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=248217 EU deputy ambassadors meet on Wednesday to settle which countries count as 'European' and what may count as 'low carbon', as the Irish EU presidency races to strike a deal among member states before the end of the year. ]]> EU deputy ambassadors will on Wednesday (11 November) debate two of the most contested parts of the bloc’s flagship industrial law, which sets “Made in EU” and low-carbon rules for products bought with public money.

The Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA) aims to use public contracts and subsidies to create steady demand for cleaner, European-made industrial products.

But disagreement over which countries count as ‘European’ has delayed the file. The current Irish EU presidency, which had hoped to get member states on board by late September, is now on its third compromise text and still has no deal.

A minority of member states led by France want the list kept as short as possible, to steer as much public money as they can towards European companies.

]]> Digital Fairness Act: EU cracks down on influencer ads and manipulative app design https://euobserver.com/248072/digital-fairness-act-eu-cracks-down-on-stealth-influencer-ads-and-manipulative-app-design/ Tue, 10 Nov 2026 15:31:08 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=248072 The Digital Fairness Act aims to impose stricter protections for people online. While the leaked draft proposes to ban overly-complicated choices to refuse data-sharing, it does not ban addictive design practises outright, warns rights watchdog EDRi. Meanwhile, online retailer Omio have complained that compliance will be costly to businesses.]]> The European Commission is set to unveil new rules on Wednesday (11 November) to prevent people from being manipulated by companies and influencers – but digital rights experts have said the legislation doesn’t go far enough.

According to a leak of the draft legislation, seen by EUobserver, the Digital Fairness Act (DFA) imposes more controls on how social media influencers can market products, while combatting dark patterns designed to manipulate consumers online.

In 2022, an EU Commission study found that 97 percent of the most popular websites and apps used by consumers employed dark patterns – intentional design choices to manipulate users towards choices that are more profitable for companies.

The DFA proposal aims to require that social media influencers state sponsorship deals by prominently labelling advertisements using terms such as “advertisement” or “commercial collaboration”, where influencers cannot misrepresent such adverts as a personal endorsement.

“People expect that influencers provide genuine advice or tips, not to be quietly sold the latest anti-wrinkle cream or fashionable outfit,” said Agustín Reyna, director general of consumer rights body BEUC. “If someone is promoting products on social media, it should be clearly stated.”

The draft also proposes a complete ban on misrepresenting information about products, or sending fake message notifications suggesting someone has been in touch when really, nobody messaged.

“Digital markets have for too long left consumers feeling disempowered and frustrated in a maze of complex cancellation processes for subscriptions they do not want, untransparent ticket pricing, or ‘low stock’ warnings that pressure them,” Reyna added.

The draft legislation forbids misleading choices about data-sharing or cookies which present refusal as the wrong choice or use deliberately confusing phrases. And the wording of the leaked act also says that cancelling an online subscription should be easy.

Opt-out for addictive features

The DFA proposal would only ban personalised advertising and pricing if likely to cause harm and if the consumer is vulnerable.

And it does not set out to ban addictive features like autoplay or infinite scrolling unless users actively switch off these features.

“That leaves significant uncertainty and potentially lengthy case-by-case assessments,” said Itxaso Domínguez de Olazábal, senior policy advisor at rights watchdog EDRi. “Why recognise the problem of addictive design so explicitly without introducing stronger obligations to prevent it?”

“Offering an opt-out should not automatically be considered sufficient,” she said. 

Read more

What is ‘coordinated inauthentic behaviour’ – and how is it distorting Europe’s online democracy?

However, Domínguez de Olazábal called it a “significant step” that “the commission’s proposal creates binding rules against manipulative design, banning fake message notifications, repeated pressure to reverse choices and deliberately complicated refusal mechanisms.”

]]> As many Russians killed near Pokrovsk in Ukraine as Soviet troops killed in the 1945 Battle of Berlin, according to hacked data (Ukraine Battlefield update, Day 1,720) https://euobserver.com/248106/as-many-russians-killed-near-pokrovsk-in-ukraine-as-soviet-troops-killed-in-the-1945-battle-of-berlin-according-to-hacked-data-ukraine-battlefield-update-day-1720/ Tue, 10 Nov 2026 14:56:54 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=248106 The data leak reveals a war so costly that battles around Pokrovsk now rival some of the most arrowing clashes of WW2, potentially reshaping how Moscow and Kyiv — as well as their allies — calculate their next moves on the front. ]]>
  • Belarusian and Ukrainian hackers obtained data on dead Russian soldiers from Russia’s statistics agency.
  • Russian data shows 400,000 Russians have been killed in total
  • They show that 74,000 Russian soldiers had been killed in Pokrovsk by December. More Ukrainians, however, died near Robotyne.
  • The brother of Zelensky adviser Mykhailo Podolyak was also killed fighting for Russia.
  • Chart of the day: Number of Ukrainian attacks using Neptune, Flamingo and Storm Shadow missiles.
  • Videos of the day: an attack on the Rubicon base more than 100 km from the front line; an owl fascinated by a drone.

    • Since the start of the invasion of Ukraine, more Russian soldiers have been killed than in all other Soviet and Russian wars since the Second World War combined. This already exceeds the number of US soldiers killed in the Second World War.

    In reality, the war has thus killed at least one percent of Russia’s male population aged 18 to 60.

    This follows from data on the number of Russian soldiers killed, published over the weekend by two hacking groups. The Belarusian pro-opposition group Cyber Partisans and Ukrainian hackers Silent Crow wrote that they had hacked Russia’s statistics agency, Rosstat, and obtained 23 terabytes of data.

    These included records of deaths in Russia in recent years. The data can be used to reconstruct the number of Russian soldiers killed since the beginning of the invasion.

    “In terms of Russian losses, this is the biggest information leak,” German economist Janis Kluge, who researches Russia’s wartime economy and military recruitment, told The Guardian newspaper.

    ]]>         EU Commission to host security talks after week of bomb hoaxes that hit 20 airports and dozens of European flights https://euobserver.com/248019/eu-commission-to-host-security-talks-after-week-of-bomb-hoaxes-that-hit-20-airports-and-dozens-of-european-flights/ Tue, 10 Nov 2026 14:47:21 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=248019 Experts from EU member states will meet on Wednesday to discuss last week’s bomb hoaxes affecting dozens of flights across Europe and causing millions in losses.]]> Experts from EU member states will meet on Wednesday (11 November) to discuss last week’s spate of bomb hoaxes which affected dozens of flights across Europe and causing millions in losses.

    The meeting, chaired by the European Commission and also including security experts from non-EU Norway, Switzerland, and Iceland, will serve to review the situation and discuss the need for extra measures.

    At least 35 planes between various airports across Europe faced bomb threats last week, according to Eurocontrol, an organisation for safe air navigation. A Finnair flight between Helsinki and Rome was escorted by Italian fighter jets while another plane, from Dublin to Rome, was diverted to a French air base.

    The scare affected a total of 20 airports in 16 countries, Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, Denmark, Finland, France, Greece, Ireland, Italy, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Serbia, Spain, and the UK.

    The bomb hoaxes affected in total less than 0.5 percent of European flights on any of the three days when alarms were sent, Eurocontrol told EUobserver, and so they “have not had an impact on the delay in the air traffic network.”

    “We remain at full operational readiness,” said EU transport commissioner Apostolos Tzitzikostas last week. “Our priority is clear: the safety of passengers and the smooth functioning of European aviation”.

    Read more

    Fake bomb warnings are hitting European aviation – but the bigger threat came from Jared Kushner

    Though none of the threats turned out to be real, each alarm consumed resources, time, energy, money, and personnel involved, costing €55,000 on average according to Eurocontrol data, but sometimes reaching even €220,000 per flight affected, according to aviation expert Philippe Baum of Coventry University. This means millions of euros lost across the continent.

    ]]>         The Kraków shooting: A Polish tragedy, a Russian opportunity https://euobserver.com/248113/the-krakow-shooting-a-polish-tragedy-a-russian-opportunity/ Tue, 10 Nov 2026 14:41:57 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=248113 As soon as a few images of the perpetrator and the contents of the boot of his car appeared in the media, the Russian propaganda machine was set to work.]]> This may be a hazard of the profession of analysing Russian information warfare, but it is sometimes dazzling to observe how Moscow’s propaganda campaigns are compelled to navigate resonant current affairs and to interpret them – whatever the actual facts – in a light favourable to the Kremlin’s foreign-policy interests.

    This obviously requires a high degree of creativity on the part of Russian propagandists, or suggests to us a boundless space of imagination in which they operate.

    The most tragic events in Poland, where 24-year-old Michał Oksiński killed both of his parents and his sister at home in the town of Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski and then drove to central Kraków and shot dead six people (four Polish nationals, a Briton, and an Austrian), wounding 16 more, offer a case in point.

    As soon as a few images of the perpetrator and the contents of the boot of his car appeared in the media, the Russian propaganda machine was set to work.

    One image showed the perpetrator’s bullet-resistant vest with a patch depicting a modern version of the flag of the early-18th-century pirate Edward Teach, known as “Blackbeard” – a morale patch widely used across the West today.

    Russian propagandists immediately – but wrongly – interpreted the patch as the symbol of the US military lifestyle brand “Forward Observations Group”, whose representatives travelled to Ukraine during the Russian-Ukrainian war.

    ]]>         [Interview] Italy’s Meloni is EU’s best hope of charming Putin at Ukraine peace talks, former Russian spy says https://euobserver.com/248018/interview-italys-meloni-is-eus-best-hope-of-charming-putin-in-ukraine-peace-talks-former-russian-spy-says/ Tue, 10 Nov 2026 14:19:42 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=248018 Any EU envoy for peace talks with Russia should meet four criteria, the Russian ex-spy said: no border with Russia, no conflicts of interest, no fear of Donald Trump, and willingness to "bloody" Vladimir Putin's nose. ]]> Italian prime minister Giorgia Meloni is Europe’s best hope of charming Russian president Vladimir Putin into a viable peace deal, a former Russian spy believes, but there is no sign yet that Putin wants to stop the Ukraine war.

    “Meloni has charisma. She’s decisive and unpredictable,” said Sergei (full name withheld), who is a retired officer from Russia’s SVR foreign intelligence service.

    “She can be reckless and Putin can relate to that … Yes. Meloni definitely interests him,” he told EUobserver.

    The 27 EU leaders will discuss the creation of a high-level Russia envoy at a summit in Dublin on Friday (13 November), after Meloni complained to EU Council president António Costa that European diplomacy on Ukraine was a mess.

    For the time being, at least seven officials (from France, Germany, Italy, the UK, the European Commission, the EU Council, and Nato) are representing Europe at US-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine, taking place in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday and Wednesday (10-11 November).

    But the EU aims to anoint a more senior Russia negotiator or group of negotiators at its next formal summit on 17 December, amid US president Donald Trump’s new promise of an imminent peace deal.

    “We have an agreement of 26, which is a tremendous achievement,” said Irish finance minister Simon Harris after meeting with his counterparts in Brussels.

    Earlier in the day, Harris said the vast majority supported the deal and that member states were “not worlds apart” and “inches away”, before adjourning the meeting “to take stock” for another round of bilateral talks after Finland, Estonia and Malta still objected to the compromise. 

    But in the end, it wasn’t enough. Maltese finance minister Clyde Caruana said Malta “supports the objectives” of the reform, but said his country’s concerns “still persist”.

    He objected mainly to raising the minimum tax rate every three years in line with inflation and adjusting to differences in price levels between member states, so that countries where the cost of living is more expensive have higher floor rates.

    But according to Caruana these plans “do not provide genuine flexibility” for national conditions.

    “The proposed minimum [excise tax] rates remain well above current national levels, notwithstanding the latest changes related to nicotine pouches,” said Caruana. “Such increases risk having disproportionate effects in Malta.” 

    Estonia also objected to the indexation mechanism but accepted an Irish compromise on Monday that freezes the EU minimum rates until the law’s next revision, the date of which has not been set.

    ]]>         Listen: What can we expect from Ukraine peace talks in Abu Dhabi? https://euobserver.com/247985/listen-what-can-we-expect-from-ukraine-peace-talks-in-abu-dhabi/ Tue, 10 Nov 2026 09:22:31 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=247985 Talks on peace in Ukraine are set to continue this week in Abu Dhabi. And this time, the EU appears to have found a way into the room. But what can actually be expected from these negotiations?]]>

    Production: By Europod, in co-production with Sphera Network.

    EUobserver is proud to have an editorial partnership with Europod to co-publish the podcast series “Briefed” hosted by Léa Marchal. The podcast is available on all major platforms.

    Find the full transcript below: 

    Talks on peace in Ukraine are set to continue this week in Abu Dhabi. And this time, the EU appears to have found a way into the room. But what can actually be expected from these negotiations?

    After a period of doubts, the EU will finally be present in Abu Dhabi. According to the commission’s spokesperson, Paula Pinho, EU representatives will actually take part in meetings. That’s a change. In February, when talks were held in Geneva, the Europeans were left waiting in the corridor.

    And they were under pressure. Last week, Italian prime minister Giorgia Meloni complained about scattered initiatives from the Nordic countries or from the E3 group, which created a cacophony. She called for clarity on the EU’s place, as an entity, in these talks.

    So who will represent the EU exactly? On the EU side, it will be the chief of staff of the commission president Ursula von der Leyen, Björn Seibert, and the foreign policy adviser to European Council president António Costa, Ana Maria Boura. Both are quite used to taking part in leaders-level discussions, and both know the issues well.

    ]]>         [Investigation] Thousands deported with Frontex help never see promised EU reintegration money https://euobserver.com/246767/thousands-deported-with-frontex-help-never-see-promised-eu-reintegration-money/ Tue, 10 Nov 2026 06:00:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=246767 Internal minutes show Frontex urging national authorities and NGOs to run sensitive data past the agency before talking to journalists, even as it insists “transparency is the rule” and refuses to release basic figures on who actually got paid.]]> The EU’s border agency Frontex has spent millions helping deported migrants rebuild their lives outside Europe.     But the rollout of Frontex’ so-called voluntary returns, and its “flagship” EURP, has also been mired in other problems.

    For years, Frontex facilitated voluntary deportations of non-EU nationals without the legally required return orders. In doing so, it violated its own regulation in almost a third of the EU, according to internal documents obtained through Freedom of Information (FOI) requests.

    To date, the agency still lacks a formal channel for supporting people who, for example, do not receive the assistance they are promised.

    The internal documents also show that, in response to growing public interest in its programmes, Frontex asked national authorities to stop sharing data with journalists and researchers, potentially hindering oversight and accountability.

    When reached for comment, a spokesperson for the EU Border Agency said that “Frontex is committed to transparency.”

    “Many of the documents on which your investigation draws […] were released to you by Frontex under the EU’s access to documents rules,” the spokesperson added.

    Of the announced suspension, the spokesperson said it was only temporary. “The programme itself is not closing.”

    So-called voluntary returns are the EU’s preferred method to dispose of third-country nationals, as these deportations are significantly cheaper to arrange than forced ones.

    Of the 63,000 returns that Frontex facilitated in 2025, the agency considers two-thirds of them to be voluntary.

    Missing legal orders

    Frontex’ foray into voluntary returns started in 2020, after the agency’s governing text was updated to expand its mandate the year prior.

    The 2019 Regulation empowered Frontex to “provide assistance in relation to voluntary returns in cooperation with the member states”. This meant that national immigration authorities could now use the agency’s flight booking system to directly procure tickets for individuals who, in principle, agreed to their deportation.

    The Regulation also authorised the agency to start delivering assistance directly to returnees. As a consequence, the agency launched in 2022 a financial aid programme for deportees.

    Through EURP, Frontex has been providing thousands of euros in financial aid to deportees within six months of their expulsion. Last July, EUobserver revealed that this programme had been used to deliver assistance to at least 50 Afghans deported from the EU over the past year.

    According to the Frontex Regulation, the agency can only deport individuals if they are subject to a return decision – an administrative or court document ordering them to leave, which only member states can issue.

    A return order is necessary before a deportation because it confirms that authorities have assessed the potential risk of a pushback, which is illegal.

    It also allows the deportee to legally challenge their expulsion if they disagree with the authorities’ assessment.

    Because of the missing order, Frontex could be found complicit of violating this core principle of international law – even if the returns themselves were categorised as voluntary.

    This legal requirement was reaffirmed in December 2025, when the Court of Justice of the EU ruled that Frontex failed to check whether a Syrian family in Greece had been issued with their return orders before deporting them.

    This blunder was not a one-off. In 2024, the agency realised it had been conducting its voluntary returns without the required return decisions in nine out of the 31 European countries where it operated, spanning 27 EU member states as well as Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland.

    The absence of these orders, as officials from the Commission noted during an April 2024 meeting, meant that the agency could be contravening multiple articles of its own regulation.

    Excerpt from a report drafted by Frontex following its April 2024 meeting.

    Frontex did not immediately close this legal vacuum, choosing instead to give EU countries time to adjust first – but continuing to operate its voluntary return operations in the nine countries in question until the end of the year. Finally, in April 2025, a decision from the agency’s Executive Director Hans Leitjens made the delivery of EURP support contingent on the existence of return decisions, as required by law.

    Frontex’ flight booking system was used for the first time in a voluntary return on 14 February 2020, for one deportee from Slovenia to North Macedonia. In July 2020, charter flights were used to conduct voluntary deportations for the first time, when 209 people were flown from France to Albania over two days. Each flight cost about €49,000 – a third of what a charter forced deportation flight might cost.

    Frontex’ eager involvement in voluntary returns served the Commission’s goal of “increasing the number and share of [these] returns from Europe”, which it announced in a policy document in April 2021. Between 2021 and 2025, while the number of people returned as part of Frontex’ forced deportations went up by only 60%, Frontex-financed voluntary returns ballooned by almost 800%.

    This growth accelerated in 2022, when the agency was put in charge of EURP. The programme aimed to establish “harmonised” rules for who was eligible to receive financial aid after their deportation from the EU, as differences in what returnees would receive post-deportation were causing “issues” onboard deportation flights.

    Historically, EU member states relied on the International Organisation for Migration to deliver this aid, of which the funding comes mainly from the EU’s Asylum, Migration and Integration Fund (AMIF).

    Instead, Frontex contracted six international organisations to deliver the financial assistance on its behalf, including one Belgian NGO headed by British private security veterans.

    However, what Frontex lacked in reach, it made up for in financial resources.

    In 2024, the agency spent €35.3m on grants to its six EURP contractors, almost double the €19m it initially budgeted. By the end of 2024, virtually all EU countries, as well as Norway and Switzerland, were using the programme to deliver assistance to their deportees. 

    According to Frowin Rausis, a researcher at the University of Geneva, European states seem to rely on EURP in countries of origin where bilateral return cooperation is limited and “where returns under national responsibility are politically most contested”.

    This way, says Rausis, “countries to which people are returned avoid the domestic backlash of deportations, as their governments are not seen as failing to protect their own citizens from undignified treatment.”

    Out of sight, out of mind

    Behind this facade, however, many returnees find themselves completely abandoned once they step off the plane back home.

    Currently, Frontex does not have a formal mechanism for handling issues from individuals who signed up to EURP – especially in cases where they do not receive the financial aid in question.

    Austrian newspaper Der Standard spoke to three people who have returned from Austria to Syria on flights arranged by Frontex after January 2025. None of them knew that Frontex was in charge of paying for their flight or the funding they were due to receive after. Two of them never received the assistance they say they were promised, even after they approached the national authorities that deported them.

    Sebastian Sperner, legal advisor at the Vienna-based migrant rights NGO Asylkoordination, said that returnees have effectively no enforceable pathway to obtain this assistance – especially once they leave EU territory.

    “You don’t have a legal title or a court ruling granting or guaranteeing that you should get this money. From both a legal and a factual perspective, it seems highly unlikely that such a claim could be asserted in an Austrian court,” he explained.

    Over the past year, Sperner’s organisation was informed of a number of cases where returnees were in a similar predicament. “I don’t see any way of actually enforcing your eligibility to get this assistance, other than pleading to the good faith of the involved actors.”

    “With the consent of the persons concerned,” a Frontex spokesperson said, “we can look into their cases with the Austrian authorities.”

    But, based on the agency’s response, keeping Frontex out of the equation seems to be by design: “People experiencing a problem with assistance they have been granted can raise it with the reintegration partner or the member state that referred them.”

Syrians were only the second largest recipients of Frontex’ aid in 2025, according to a presentation given by the agency earlier this year.

    As part of this investigation, we asked Frontex for a breakdown of its EURP beneficiaries for the past two years, in order to determine which nationalities were predominantly impacted by missing aid delivery.     “Frontex is not in position to provide the disaggregated data per year and nationality of a member state to the general public without explicit consent from the member state in question,” the spokesperson said in an email. The spokesperson did not provide a reason why.

    The European Commission is now scrambling to get an additional €50m from other sources to plug the EURP funding gap.

    When it comes to Gaza, an Eisenkot-led government might be more open to supporting the implementation of the UN Security Council-approved Gaza peace plan, but it will condition its cooperation and the Israeli Defence Forces’ withdrawal from most of the Strip on full disarmament of [Palestinian militant group] Hamas.

    These caveats notwithstanding, and as a result of external pressure, agreement may eventually be found to reverse the most egregious policies of the Netanyahu era in the West Bank, notably by curbing unscrupulous settlement expansion, halting the ‘E1’ settlement project, dismantling illegal settler outposts in Area C, holding terrorist settlers to account and ending the punitive withholding of clearance revenues from the Palestinian Authority, estimated to be between $4.6bn [€4.1bn] and $6bn. 

    However, it is far from clear whether Eisenkot and his hawkish allies on the center-right will want to pursue a different approach towards Iran and Lebanon.

    While they have criticised Netanyahu for starting the war against Teheran without political exit strategy they full-heartedly support aggressive military action against the Mullah regime [in Iran] and [the Lebanese paramilitary force] Hezbollah.

    Netanyahu knows this as well and might resume military strikes on Iran and its allies in the region while still in power.

    The Washington dynamic

    Predicting the trajectory of US Middle East policy under president Donal Trump, now constrained by a Democrat-dominated Congress, remains complex. While Trump retains broad constitutional prerogatives in foreign policy, the new Congress holds significant leverage through budgetary legislation.

    The announced phase-out of the nearly $4bn in annual US military aid to Israel by Trump is a clear indicator of shifting domestic political winds.

    Given the increasingly negative image of Israel among Democratic voters and politicians, it is improbable that the new Congress will approve further unconditional multi-annual, large-scale military aid.

    The conflict with Tehran introduces a more volatile variable. While the US Constitution demands congressional approval for a declaration of war, Trump might argue that strikes against Iran constitute independent defensive actions necessary to protect American lives and interests, thereby bypassing congressional oversight.

    With no further electoral hurdles until November 2028, Trump faces limited political restraint at home, short of an unlikely impeachment proceeding.

    Read more

    Trump’s mid-term election disaster is not good news for Nato or Ukraine

    Should Trump initiate massive military action the Iranian regime will, in all likelihood, respond by triggering a retaliatory cycle that would inevitably target Gulf states harboring US military assets, including civilian energy infrastructure and desalination plants.

    As witnessed in the past six months, collateral damage reverberates far beyond the region.

    The economic impact is felt globally, hitting US households and European economies alike. Tehran’s strategic calculus remains rooted in the belief that substantial financial and economic costs will compel US partners worldwide to exert pressure on the Trump administration to seek a political, rather than military, solution.

    Furthermore, domestic pressure within the US will likely grow. The non-interventionist MAGA wing, recognising the potential impact on future electoral bids, such as US vice-president JD Vance’s potential 2028 presidential campaign, is increasingly wary of the costs associated with prolonged conflict.

    This also implies revisiting the special relationship with Israel, increasingly seen as a liability for US interests in the region and beyond.

    When combined with the nearly unified opposition from the Democratic party, the political sustainability of massive military intervention in the Gulf is questionable.

    Read more

    G7 releases diesel stocks after Trump pressure, EU denies caving

    Europe’s strategic failure and the path forward

    How can Europe meaningfully impact policy decisions in Tel Aviv, Washington, and the Gulf capitals? The answer requires a twofold, simultaneous approach.

    First, Europe must abandon its muted, reactive diplomacy. It is entirely appropriate to wait until a new government in Tel Aviv is sworn in and congressional races are validated before initiating formal, high-level engagement.

    However, nothing prevents European politicians, parliamentarians and senior officials from pro-actively reaching out to the forces in Israel, the US, and the Gulf that are seeking an end to military conflicts and sustainable political solutions.

    This engagement must emphasize, above all, the imperative of respecting international law as the foundation for any lasting resolution, particularly in the longest-entrenched conflict theatre: occupied Palestine.

    Also, on Iran and the contentious issue of its nuclear programme, the EU has much to offer, having played a critical role in the negotiations that led to the landmark JCPOA agreement with Iran in 2015 on non nuclear non-proliferation.

    Getting there again might probably be the best political outcome one could hope for in view of de-escalation and stability.

    Second, for the EU to regain credibility, it must match its rhetoric with substantive action. It is long overdue for European institutions and member states to fulfill their own obligations under international and European law.

    This requires, inter alia, the immediate banning of trade with Israel’s illegal settlements, in view of the International Court of Justice’s (ICJ’s) advisory opinion of 19 July 2024.

    Read more

    No Israeli bonds on sale in EU for now, in de facto €2.2bn sanction

    Furthermore, the EU must impose sanctions on ministers of the outgoing government, specifically Ben Gvir and Smotrich, for their policies and conduct in Gaza and the West Bank.

    Importantly, in light of the ICJ’s 2024 binding provisional measures under the Genocide Convention and the ongoing military actions in Gaza that contravene basic norms of international humanitarian law, halting the export of military goods and equipment to Israel is a legal and political imperative. 

    These measures target explicitly the outgoing caretaker government of Netanyahu and represent necessary, long overdue steps to uphold the EU’s obligations under international law and its own Association Agreement.

    Read more

    Leaked memo: EU has known since 2017 it had legal right to freeze Israel trade deal

    They also serve as a warning that the EU means business when insisting on respecting and applying international law, including towards its allies.

    Once the new Israeli government takes office, the EU should formally propose a critical, time-bound dialogue regarding the application of the relevant provisions of the EU-Israel Association Agreement, establishing clear human rights benchmarks against which future conduct will be monitored.

    The lesson at this juncture is unequivocal. Following the elections in Israel and the US, a window for change has opened.

    The EU cannot afford to remain a bystander, squandering the opportunity for shaping policy decisions in Tel Aviv and Washington.

    It has already paid a high price for the ignorance and lack of courage of most of its leaders who, for far too long, refrained from acting against the disastrous policies of the Netanyahu and Trump administrations.

    The time for proactive, principled and bold European action is now.

    ]]>         The clock is ticking: Europe is running out of time to save the International Criminal Court  https://euobserver.com/247689/the-clock-is-ticking-europe-is-running-out-of-time-to-save-the-international-criminal-court/ Mon, 09 Nov 2026 11:59:01 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=247689 The US midterms have opened a political window for Europe. With a key US licence expiring in April 2027, Brussels must turn its rhetorical support for the ICC into concrete action before this opportunity closes.]]> The European Commission has so far been cautious about using the EU’s Blocking Statute to protect the International Criminal Court (ICC) from US sanctions. On 14 October, it said discussions were continuing. Nine days later, it advised European companies to continue providing services to the Court, relying on temporary US authorisations and ongoing diplomacy. That is not a durable strategy.

    On 9 October, the Trump administration placed the ICC itself on the US sanctions list.

    Europe must now decide whether it is prepared to defend the independence of an international court in practice, not just in words.

    The immediate deadline is 7 April 2027. The broad US general licence currently authorising transactions necessary to maintain the Court’s operations expires on that date.

    It covers essential activities such as salaries, insurance, contributions by States Parties and routine commercial services. Three other US licences cover more specific areas, including telecommunications and software, pensions and certain transactions involving ICC detainees.

    They do not share the same expiry date. But General License 13 provides the broad operational breathing space on which the Court currently depends.

    Washington has presented this six-month period as an opportunity for States Parties to address its concerns. These include withdrawing arrest warrants against Israeli leaders, formally closing the Afghanistan investigation insofar as it concerns alleged crimes by US personnel, and changing the Rome Statute to prevent the Court from exercising jurisdiction over US nationals, even where alleged crimes are committed on the territory of a State Party.

    The principle at stake is fundamental: the ICC’s jurisdiction is established by law, not by the political preferences of governments. A court forced to trade judicial independence for the ability to operate cannot fulfil its mandate.

    Read more

    EU bets on diplomacy, not blocking statute, to protect ICC from Trump sanctions

    A political opening in Washington

    The Democrats have won control of both chambers of the US Congress in the midterm elections. The new Congress takes office in January.

    President Donald Trump retains his veto, so a legislative reversal of the sanctions is unlikely. But an opposition-controlled Congress can hold hearings, exercise oversight and scrutinise the costs of the sanctions for American banks and technology companies.

    Brussels should not assume that the Democrats are natural allies. In January 2025, 45 House Democrats voted for a Republican bill to sanction the ICC. Senate Democrats subsequently blocked it, partly because of concerns about its breadth and its consequences for US businesses and allies.

    Europe’s strongest argument in Washington is therefore not simply defence of the Netanyahu arrest warrants. It is that a president is using emergency economic powers to target an independent court and the companies that serve it, damaging American interests and relations with its allies.

    The pressure goes further. In July, at a closed-door meeting of Nato ambassadors in Brussels, US ambassador Matthew Whitaker urged allies to withdraw from the Rome Statute and end material support for the ICC, according to reporting on a US diplomatic document. This was an American demand, not a Nato position. Every Nato member except the United States and Türkiye is a party to the Rome Statute. They should not be pressured into abandoning their commitment to the Court.

    The legal instrument Brussels must prepare

    The EU Blocking Statute, Regulation 2271/96, protects European operators against the extraterritorial application of specified foreign laws. It prohibits companies within its scope from complying with listed sanctions. But it cannot eliminate the commercial risks for companies exposed to the US market, nor guarantee that Washington will not retaliate.

    The Dutch foreign minister, Tom Berendsen, has called it a “nuclear option”, while insisting that Europe should prepare to use it. That distinction matters. Preparing the instrument does not mean activating it immediately. It means ensuring that Europe can act quickly if diplomacy fails.

    There is a legal step Brussels cannot avoid: the US measures do not automatically fall within the Statute’s current scope.

    The commission must prepare a delegated act adding the relevant measures to its annex, subject to the applicable EU scrutiny procedures. That work should begin now, not in the weeks before the deadline.

    There is already a political mandate. The European Council has reaffirmed support for the ICC and called for uninterrupted access to financial and other services. France has said it is prepared to support the use of the Blocking Statute if necessary; Belgium has called for the commission to prepare for its possible activation.

    The European Parliament’s foreign affairs committee has backed activation and practical protection for the Court, while the ICC has been named the 2026 Sakharov Prize laureate.

    Read more

    International Criminal Court wins EU’s top human rights prize in defiance of Trump’s sanctions

    On 23 October, the commission advised operators to continue providing services, noting that General License 13 currently authorises necessary transactions and that SEPA payments rely on European infrastructure.

    These are welcome steps, but they do not provide a lasting safeguard once the broad US licence expires.

    Read more

    ‘Bullies cannot be appeased’: Pressure mounts on EU to shield ICC from new US sanctions

    What Europe should do

    Prepare the legal instrument. The commission should draft the delegated act adding the relevant US measures to the Blocking Statute’s annex, consult Member States and complete the preparatory work well ahead of April. Preparation is not activation; it gives Europe the option to act without delay.

    Protect European service providers. Banks, insurers, payment providers and IT companies need clear guidance and political backing if they are targeted. The commission and member states should identify vulnerable services and ensure the Court can continue paying staff, receiving contributions and maintaining essential infrastructure.

    Build an international coalition. Nine countries — Australia, Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands and the United Kingdom — have issued a joint declaration supporting the Court. The coalition should expand to include other EU members and the nine non-EU countries that aligned themselves with the EU statement: Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Moldova, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Norway and Ukraine. Together, they could coordinate financial, insurance and IT support, share the costs of essential services and assist staff and providers exposed to sanctions. The challenge is to turn political solidarity into practical protection.

    Talk to Washington but draw a red line. The Rome Statute already recognises the primacy of genuine national investigations and prosecutions through the principle of complementarity. Dialogue is essential, but concessions on the Court’s jurisdiction or arrest warrants are not acceptable. Nor should Europe entertain amendments that place powerful states and their nationals beyond the reach of international criminal justice.

    Take the case to Capitol Hill. European governments should engage the incoming congressional leadership, relevant committee chairs and American companies. The argument should focus on the costs to US businesses, the interests of allies and the damage to the rule of law. The immediate request should be to extend the broad general licence and keep the Court’s essential operations authorised.

    The midterms have created an opening, not a guarantee of change. Congress may scrutinise the sanctions, but Europe cannot rely on it to reverse them. The choice is not between diplomacy and defending the ICC. Europe must do both. Preparing its legal and practical safeguards is what will make diplomacy credible.

    If Brussels waits for Washington to change course, it may discover that the temporary authorisation has expired before Europe has a response. The question is no longer whether Europe supports the ICC. It is whether it is prepared to act before time runs out.

]]> Une entreprise peut réussir sans jamais annoncer de levée de fonds. Une affirmation qui résonne plus particulièrement après trois années de correction du capital-risque : de plus de 13 milliards d’euros en 2022, les montants levés par les startups françaises sont revenus à 6,8 milliards en 2025, selon notre recensement MaddyMoney. Avec le retour des exigences de rentabilité, les ventes et la solidité du modèle économique reprennent leur place dans l’appréciation d’un parcours entrepreneurial.

Le commerce en ligne offre précisément un moyen de bâtir une entreprise à partir de ses clients : proposer un produit, trouver des acheteurs et réinvestir les revenus pour développer l’activité. L’ambition peut être de vivre de son savoir-faire, de gagner en autonomie ou de recruter à mesure que les commandes progressent. Les plateformes de e-commerce et l’IA rendent ce parcours plus accessible, en simplifiant la création d’une boutique et une partie de sa gestion.

Tester une idée avant d’élargir son activité

Choisir quelques produits, les présenter, encaisser les paiements et suivre les commandes : les plateformes de e-commerce réunissent des fonctions qu’il fallait auparavant assembler ou faire développer. Selon l’étude The Entrepreneur Effect, 78 % des marchands interrogés par Shopify ont construit eux-mêmes leur boutique sur la plateforme.

Il n’est pas non plus nécessaire de démarrer avec un catalogue étendu. À l’échelle mondiale, 41 % des boutiques Shopify se lancent avec un seul produit, d’après les données de la plateforme. Une offre resserrée permet de confronter une idée aux achats réels avant d’engager davantage de moyens. En 2025, environ 1,2 million de boutiques y ont enregistré leur première vente. Ce chiffre renseigne sur les débuts d’une activité, sans préjuger de sa rentabilité ou de sa pérennité.

L’IA pour avancer avec une petite équipe

L’intelligence artificielle prolonge cette simplification. Pour Julien Tuffery, dirigeant de l’Atelier TUFFERY, enseigne de jeans et vêtements Made in France, « l’IA est d’ores et déjà très présente dans notre quotidien. Nous l’utilisons pour analyser plus rapidement les données, structurer et synthétiser les informations, travailler dans différentes langues, et nous aider dans certaines tâches techniques. Pour une entreprise de notre taille, cela nous donne accès à des capacités qui, auparavant, auraient nécessité beaucoup plus de ressources. »

Sidekick, l’assistant IA de Shopify, joue ce rôle en effectuant de nombreuses tâches, telles que réaliser des calculs, écrire du code, effectuer des recherches sur Internet et mémoriser les informations que lui transmet un marchand. Pour une personne qui lance son activité, l’intérêt est concret : disposer d’une aide pour prendre en main les outils, sans devoir maîtriser chaque fonction dès le départ.

L’IA contribue également à rééquilibrer la concurrence entre petites et grandes marques. En permettant aux consommateurs de rechercher des produits correspondant à des attentes très précises, les assistants IA ouvrent de nouvelles possibilités de visibilité aux enseignes spécialisées, indépendamment de leur notoriété. Selon Shopify, 75 % des ventes attribuées à des recommandations par IA proviennent de boutiques vendant des produits situés hors des 100 catégories les plus courantes. Pour ces entreprises, l’enjeu n’est donc plus seulement d’être connues, mais d’être identifiées comme pertinentes et fiables dans leur domaine. Cela suppose de proposer des informations produits détaillées, des contenus de qualité et une expertise clairement identifiable.

Une évolution que constate Camille Becerra, fondatrice et dirigeante d’Anatae, marque française de thé matcha japonais 100 % biologique et naturel : « Cela a changé notre façon d’envisager le contenu. Les outils d’IA valorisent l’expertise et les informations précises et vérifiables. Nous continuons donc à investir dans des contenus éducatifs sur le thé japonais et veillons à ce que chaque fiche produit indique clairement le cépage, la région, la certification et les analyses en laboratoire. Être la référence dans notre domaine est aujourd’hui plus que jamais une stratégie d’acquisition, et pas seulement une stratégie de marque. »

« Demain, certains de nos clients ne taperont peut-être plus “jeans Made in France” dans un moteur de recherche ; ils demanderont peut-être simplement à une IA quels jeans fabriqués en France ils devraient choisir, complète Julien Tuffery. Cela modifie inévitablement la manière dont une marque doit envisager sa visibilité en ligne. »

Des retombées au-delà de la boutique

Atelier TUFFERY illustre la façon dont le commerce en ligne peut permettre à une entreprise locale de se développer sans quitter son territoire. Depuis Florac, au cœur des Cévennes, la manufacture fondée en 1892 vend désormais ses produits directement en France et dans le monde entier.

« Le web nous a permis de dépasser notre isolement géographique sans jamais avoir à nous déraciner, explique Julien Tuffery. Nous pouvons développer une activité nationale et internationale tout en continuant à fabriquer nos produits là où l’entreprise est née. Aujourd’hui, une commande passée à Paris, Londres, Tokyo ou à l’autre bout du monde peut contribuer directement au développement de notre manufacture et à l’économie d’une région profondément rurale. Le commerce en ligne n’a pas détourné la création de valeur de notre territoire. Au contraire, il nous a donné les moyens de rester ici, d’investir ici et de nous développer ici. »

Cette croissance produit des effets concrets dans les Cévennes. L’entreprise a créé plus de 40 emplois, principalement à Florac et dans les environs. Sa manufacture et sa boutique ont accueilli plus de 40 000 visiteurs au cours des douze derniers mois, tandis que son activité e-commerce génère plus de 20 000 colis par an, contribuant ainsi à l’activité du bureau de poste local.

À l’échelle nationale, Shopify estime que les entreprises qui utilisent sa plateforme ont généré 21,5 milliards d’euros d’activité économique en France et soutenu environ 115 000 emplois entre le 1er juillet 2025 et le 30 juin 2026. Ces estimations reposent sur une modélisation qui tient compte des effets directs, indirects et induits de l’activité des marchands et des partenaires de Shopify.

L’accès à des clients étrangers élargit encore ces retombées. Les ventes transfrontalières des marchands Shopify établis en France ont progressé de 314 % entre 2022 et l’année achevée le 30 juin 2026. Pour les entrepreneurs, vendre à l’étranger demande toujours d’organiser la livraison et le service client. Mais la technologie leur permet désormais de développer une activité internationale tout en restant concentrés sur leur savoir-faire et profondément ancrés dans leur territoire.

« Chaque jour, des entrepreneurs transforment un savoir-faire ou une ambition en une activité concrète, qui crée de l’emploi et participe à la dynamique des territoires, souligne Alexandre Chaumien, responsable des revenus pour l’Europe du Sud chez Shopify. Avec la technologie et l’IA, on leur donne le pouvoir d’aller encore plus loin et de voir encore plus grand. Ces opportunités pour eux le sont aussi pour l’économie française. »

      <title>US inflation rose 0.4% in October as price increases cooled and gas costs dipped</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/10/october-inflation-report</link>
      <description><p>New data comes after Republicans’ midterms losses – which were largely seen as a rebuke of the party over high prices</p><p>US inflation rose 0.4% from September to October, slightly above expectations but still a cooldown in price increases as the cost of gas dipped during the month.</p><p>The Bureau of Labor Statistics did not release the usual year-over-year inflation figure as part of the consumer price index (CPI), which measures the price of a basket of goods and services, as data was not collected in October 2025 during the government shutdown.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/10/october-inflation-report">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Senators pressured Danielle Thumann, senior counsel to FCC chair Brendan Carr, to speak about agency’s actions toward ABC and Jimmy Kimmel</p><p>During a contentious Tuesday hearing on her nomination by Donald Trump to serve as a Federal Communications Commission (FCC) commissioner, Senate Democrats hammered Danielle Thumann about recent actions taken by the Brendan Carr-led regulator that have been criticized as hostile to press freedom.</p><p>Thumann, who serves as senior counsel to Carr, is expected to be approved as commissioner, with Republicans in charge of the US Senate and House.       <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/10/oil-prices-fall-donald-trump-iran-war-ftse-100-markets</link>
      <description><p>Brent crude drops below $90 and markets climb after president downplays prospect of further strikes</p><p>Oil prices have fallen to the lowest level since late August while stock markets climbed higher, as markets reacted with relief to <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/09/trump-iran-war">Donald Trump saying that the war on Iran is “effectively over”</a>.</p><p>Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, fell nearly 3% to $89.66, the lowest since 31 August, on Tuesday morning, after the US president downplayed the need for military action against Iran “at this point”. The fall came after a near 6% drop on Monday on signs that the conflict might be nearing an end.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/10/oil-prices-fall-donald-trump-iran-war-ftse-100-markets">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>US job growth exceeds expectations in October despite economic uncertainty</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/06/us-job-growth-october</link>
      <description><p>‘Low-hire, low-fire’ labor market shows sluggish growth but few layoffs, with an interest rate hike expected in December</p><p>The US added 165,000 jobs to the economy in October, a sign of resilience in the labor market amid war in the Middle East and inflation, according to new data released on Friday.</p><p>Economists had said the labor market has been stuck in a “low-hire, low-fire” state, in which job growth is sluggish but layoffs also remain low, but October’s data surpassed economist expectations. The <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/usemployment">unemployment rate</a> went down slightly to 4.1%, the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) reported.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/06/us-job-growth-october">Continue reading...</a></description>

<![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comWed, 11 Nov 2026 06:54:27 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[Is the European Union getting real about ending tech dependence?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/big-tech/2026/11/11/is-the-european-union-getting-real-about-ending-tech-dependence/https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/big-tech/2026/11/11/is-the-european-union-getting-real-about-ending-tech-dependence/Wed, 11 Nov 2026 06:00:01 +0000

Europeans are afraid – very afraid – of their dependence on foreign digital technology.

A recent poll by the Bertelsmann Foundation finds almost three-quarters of European Union (EU) citizens worry that critical digital services “could be remotely disabled by actors outside Europe”. The same overwhelming majority think it important Europe should have “control over key digital technologies”.

As in other cases (such as Europeans’ negative reactions to the EU trade “deal” with Donald Trump last year), the bloc’s citizens are clear about what they want – and it’s not what they are getting at the moment. So how are European governments, and the EU in particular, going about delivering the “control” that voters demand?

Europe depends on other economies for much of the digital technology “stack”: the US for software, Taiwan for microchips, China for swathes of hardware. A first question, then, is how much of the stack needs to be home-grown inside the EU.

When I ask this of Henna Virkkunen, the European Commission vice-president in charge of tech sovereignty, she lists AI (artificial intelligence) models, semiconductors, quantum technology, satellites and the cloud as areas where Europe needs its own productive capacity. She does not go as far as self-sufficiency; the objective is “that we shouldn’t have risky dependencies [or be] dependent on one company or one third country”.

That is an ambitious list of sectors nonetheless, given how far behind Europe is. It is certainly sufficiently demanding that we must ask whether pursuing it would come at the cost of falling further behind and of giving up foreign frontier technology for the sake of inferior home-made versions. What does Brussels think about that trade-off?

US voters have rejected data centres and AI. What happens now?

It may not be that dramatic, Virkkunen suggests. “Sometimes we know that some companies ... want to give the impression that they always have the best services and the competitors don’t ... and it’s not always true,” she tells me.

She argues that the home-grown alternatives are sometimes just smaller and lesser known, rather than uncompetitive on quality or price. But that means the public sector can catalyse domestic substitutes by playing its role as a customer right.

Is the European public sector doing that, though? Many smaller EU-based digital companies feel they have a good product but government customers prefer to stick with the big providers they are used to. The commissioner accepts there is a degree of inertia. There is also a need to be “creative”, she says, to facilitate smaller companies coming together in consortiums to provide the scale of supply needed.

The biggest challenge, though, is access to funding for EU tech companies – not because of a lack of savings but thanks to Europe’s failure to channel financing to risky ventures. While 182,130 homes have been granted planning permission over the last five years, historical Central Bank data indicate that 25 to 32 per cent of planning permissions never commenced construction.

“If we assume the same lapse ratio as the Central Bank analysis, this shortfall sits between 123,400 and 136,100 homes,” the report said.

]]><![CDATA[Dublin city centre evolving to meet strength of hotel demand from visitors and investors]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/property/commercial-property/2026/11/11/dublin-city-centre-evolving-to-meet-strength-of-hotel-demand-from-visitors-and-investors/https://www.irishtimes.com/property/commercial-property/2026/11/11/dublin-city-centre-evolving-to-meet-strength-of-hotel-demand-from-visitors-and-investors/Wed, 11 Nov 2026 05:35:00 +0000Few European cities kept their hotels as full as Dublin did this year. Occupancy reached nearly 85 per cent in the 12 months to September, according to CoStar, despite the headwinds facing global travel in 2026.

To understand the trend properly, I looked at visitor and occupancy data and spoke to a number of hoteliers. A decline in visitor numbers followed the outbreak of war in Iran and ran into early spring while the World Cup in the US had an impact on the tourist spend that would ordinarily have come to Ireland in early summer. However, the market recovered strongly through the rest of the busy season and beyond, and the data bears that out.

I attended the Irish Tourism Industry Confederation (ITIC) conference at Dublin’s Convention Centre in October to get a better sense of sentiment across the sector. The feedback from operators at the conference broadly reflected this view. The confederation highlighted a slight year-on-year decline in North American visitor numbers during August, which was attributed to fewer US travellers visiting for the College Football Classic than in previous years.

The issue of hotel room rates is more complex. According to CoStar, average room rates grew by 1.3 per cent in the nine months to September compared with 2025, with the average daily rate (ADR) reaching €177.80, a strong level for a market running at such high occupancy. This growth has not kept pace with Ireland’s consumer price index, however, which has run at more than 3 per cent over the same period.

Overall, the fact that occupancy held at such a high level this year despite such pressures is evidence of the market’s underlying resilience. Higher fuel costs and impending increases in the price of travel are the challenge for the winter months.

Irish weather

One of the most interesting contributions at the ITIC conference came from US ambassador to Ireland Ed Walsh, who spoke about the growing appreciation Americans have for the Irish summer, particularly the one just gone. Heatwaves have become more common across southern Europe in July and August in recent years, and northern European destinations have benefited as a result. Ireland’s famously unpredictable and changeable weather may well have become one of its greatest selling points.

The ambassador was also upbeat on the prospects for Irish-American tourism. He pointed to the potential for further events such as a college basketball game to extend the event calendar into the quieter winter months.

The Ryder Cup, the NFL and a strong events pipeline

Looking ahead, the events calendar is just as encouraging. The Ryder Cup at Adare Manor will be among the largest sporting events Ireland has ever hosted, with 280,000 spectators expected, and hotels are already booking out well beyond Limerick.

Beyond golf, last year’s inaugural NFL regular season game at Croke Park was among the best weekends Dublin hoteliers have experienced over the last decade, with room rates spiking sharply across the city. The NFL is expected to return, potentially within the next two years. U2 will play an Irish date next year as part of their global tour, Dublin will host several games at Euro 2028 and the proposed 20,000-capacity arena in the docklands, being developed by OVG and Live Nation, would add a year-round source of events.

Why Dublin hotels attract capital

Demand like this has not gone unnoticed. Sustained high occupancy over the last number of years has brought increased focus from developers and investors on a sector that historically has not been considered alongside core commercial or residential assets.

Last year the Irish market saw its largest-ever hotel transaction, with Pandox, one of Europe’s largest hotel property companies, acquiring Dalata Hotel Group for about €1.4 billion, the majority of which were Irish assets. Few deals do more to show how sought-after Dublin hotels have become.

Dublin hotels are utilitarian by nature. That is, they sit beside stadiums, convention centres, the airport or other transport hubs. When one considers the convenience of their location and the ongoing undersupply of rooms in the Dublin market, it’s easy to understand how such a high level of capital was deployed in a single deal.

€1bn pipeline

That faith on the part of investors is also showing up in new supply. Dublin’s hotel stock is on course to pass 30,000 rooms for the first time by 2028, with a substantial pipeline of new bedrooms due to deliver over the next two years. At an estimated development cost of €250,000 to €300,000 per key, the committed pipeline of more than 3,500 rooms represents a gross development value of between €0.9 billion and €1.1 billion, a significant statement of confidence in the long-term fundamentals of the market. The majority of this new supply consists of budget, long-stay and midscale accommodation.

Evolving city centre

The city centre is evolving in its composition, a trend I examined in an Irish Times article in July 2024, What impact will remote working have on the future of Dublin city centre? One of the central findings was that the city would move towards a greater mix of hotel, residential and living sector uses over time. And that has increasingly been borne out.

Some developers are now repurposing city-centre buildings for hotel use, and a number of former banks and retail units have planning permission for it. The former Cafe Kylemore on O’Connell Street was recently sold with permission for a boutique hotel, and a five-star hotel is planned for the former Ulster Bank premises at College Green, to name two. Not every project materialises, however. Numbers 5-9 Frederick Street South came to market with a feasibility study showing hotel potential, but was acquired, refurbished and upgraded as an office scheme, now let to Cantor Fitzgerald.

What comes next

Adding more than 3,500 rooms to a market this full should bring some normalisation of trading levels. The events pipeline, record passenger numbers through Dublin Airport, and Fáilte Ireland’s sharp focus on growing visitor numbers all point in the right direction. Dublin remains one of the more attractive European hotel markets for investors.

Colin Richardson is a senior director and head of research at CBRE Ireland

The rule of thumb is that each 1 per cent hike in the public sector pay and pensions bill costs the exchequer roughly €370 million.

It’s unlikely to change the dial on your return, however; the relief is capped at 20 per cent of the increase, up to a maximum of €1,250. As an example, a €3,000 increase would give a tax saving of €300.

If you rented out a property in 2025, you will pay slightly less tax this year than you might have done previously, due to the increase in the Residential Premises Rental Income Relief.

First introduced in 2024, the relief is offered at a rate of 20 per cent of the landlord’s rental income. For 2025 tax returns, the limit will increase from €3,000 to €4,000. It means that the maximum credit will increase from €600 for 2024 to €800 in 2025 – and €1,000 for 2026 and 2027.

“These figures compare price changes relative to income changes over time; as such, they do not rank countries by how expensive homes are in relation to income levels in absolute terms,” Eurostat said.

Public service pensions in general make provision for a 50 per cent survivor’s pension for a spouse if the retired public servant predeceases them. It is a valuable safety net for families .

Following an enquiry from you, the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage sent you what appear to be disembodied section from various bits of legislation that are as impenetrable as this stuff usually is.

The issue here is that there are two schemes - an original one that dates back to 1956 legislation and a more recent one operating under legislation passed in the 1980s. What rights you do and do not have depend on which one covers your husband’s employment.

I am indebted to Irish Congress of Trade Unions head of social policy and employment affairs, Laura Bambrick, and a number of her colleagues in Ictu’s public service unions for guiding me through the relevant detail.

Essentially, under the original 1956 Local Government (Superannuation) Act, there was no provision for a survivor’s pension under the widow’s and orphan pension scheme in a case like yours - where you got married after your husband had retired from his public sector role.

That scheme was specifically designed to cover family relationships established during pensionable employment. Once the person was no longer contributing to the scheme - as they would not in retirement - they were not covered for any marriage that took place during their working lives, nor any child born.

However, that changed in the 1980s.

People working in the Civil Service who were appointed after September 1st, 1984 became members of a revised spouses’ and children’s pension scheme. And this scheme made specific provision that even where a marriage took place after retirement, the spouse would be entitled to a survivors’ pension.

Those pension rights were extended to local authority staff under the Local Government Officers (Spouses and Children’s Contributory Pension) Scheme, 1986, with the rights backdated to September 1st, 1984.

This is interesting because it shows that as far back as 1984, there was an understanding that there was a reasonable case for extending pension protection to spouses who, simply by accident of timing, got married after a person’s retirement.

So, if your husband started working with the local authority any time after the end of August 1984, you are entitled to a pension on the back of his employment in the event of his death.

Even if he started working with them before that date, there was an option at that time for existing employees to transfer to the new scheme. He and you would certainly need to check through his records to see if he availed of that opportunity or chose to stay with the original scheme.

The response you have got from the department does not seem to clarify that one way or the other. And one of the trade union sources notes that Article 120 of the 1998 Local Government Superannuation (Consolidation) Scheme, which was quoted to you by the Department of Housing, relates to the older Widows’ and Orphans’ arrangements.

If he was covered under the newer arrangements, it would be irrelevant.

So, first up, track down the dates when your husband started work with the local authority and when he retired. If he was employed with them before 1984, you also need to check whether he opted in to the revised arrangements that came into force at that time, or not.

I am told that the pensions section in the Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation may be able to help.
