Knot said he was ready to use the ECB’s existing crisis-fighting tools, including bond buying. “If circumstances so dictate, we won’t hesitate [to intervene],” said Knot.

The 59-year-old Dutch man, who led his country’s central bank from 2011 to 2025, was officially nominated on Friday by The Hague to succeed ECB president Christine Lagarde. She will leave the bank in early February, nine months before the end of her eight-year term.

Knot did not rule out creating additional instruments to combat future crises. If the next crisis “is different in nature” from the previous ones that led to the creation of the current tools, “I wouldn’t even exclude the fact that we would design another more tailor-made tool,” he said.

Knot’s main rival is Pablo Hernández de Cos, general manager of the Bank for International Settlements and former Spanish central bank governor, who has been nominated by Madrid.

European leaders might decide on the new ECB president at their next formal summit in late November, but the decision could also be delayed until next month.

ECB grants regulatory approval for Bawag PTSB takeover

The decision requires the consent of at least 16 of the 21 countries that use the euro, representing 65 per cent of its population.

Leaders will also have to agree on a new ECB chief economist and a new board member in charge of the markets portfolio at the central bank. The term of the current chief economist, Irish man Philip Lane, ends in May and European Central Bank governing council member Isabel Schnabel will leave to join the International Monetary Fund in January.

The ECB’s closely watched leadership reshuffle unfolds against the backdrop of a sharp surge in French government borrowing costs since the summer, with yields on its 10-year bonds briefly shooting above 5 per cent last month. The spread, or gap, to German Bunds widened to 1.75 percentage points before it came down slightly, reflecting the premium investors are demanding to hold French debt.

In reference to an infamous remark by Lagarde in early 2020 that the ECB is “not here to close spreads”, which triggered a temporary bond market sell-off, Knot said the ECB should “definitely be there to contain them [spreads] when driven by unwarranted and disorderly market dynamics”.

The Frankfurt-based institution has created “a toolkit to deal with such situations”, he argued.

These include the emergency bond-buying scheme Outright Monetary Transactions, introduced after former European Central Bank president Mario Draghi’s “whatever it takes” speech in 2012 during the euro zone sovereign debt crisis.

In 2022, the central bank also created the transmission protection instrument as it began raising interest rates to fight surging inflation.

Knot stressed that any ECB firefighting needed to be done “in a manner that does not undermine its institutional credibility”, adding that the central bank could not fix unsustainable fiscal policy.

Its current crisis-fighting tools “combine a requirement [for governments] to bring fundamentals in order with a temporary shield against unwarranted or disorderly market dynamics”, said Knot, adding that he has “always been a big proponent” of this approach.

He stressed that there was “no magic single spread level” that would trigger an intervention in bond markets from the ECB and that the central bank was right to stay on the sidelines for now.

Moreover, Knot stressed that rising government debt costs in themselves cannot justify European Central Bank bond buying.

“There is a difference between a repricing from one level to another and disorderly market dynamics with a lot of volatility and a lot of contagion across different markets,” he said, adding that the assessment of what constitutes an unwarranted and disorderly market development always involves “a healthy dose of judgment”.

Knot pushed back against public perceptions of him as a monetary policy hawk who has a preference for high interest rates.

“There are situations in which you have to pursue dovish policy, but there are also situations in which you are expected to conduct hawkish policy,” he said, adding that this was “driven by circumstances, not by personalities or predispositions”.

He noted that “dovish policy” was necessary during the Covid pandemic while the ECB had to pursue a “hawkish” one to fight surging inflation from 2022.

Over the coming months, the European Central Bank’s interest rate policy is likely to be hostage to developments in the Middle East and their impact on energy prices, he said. Policymakers in Frankfurt have increased borrowing costs in two quarter-point steps since June to 2.5 per cent.

He said that if energy prices remained roughly where they were, he saw little need for higher interest rates. “There may be a bit of extra tightening needed, but I don’t think an awful lot of it,” Knot said, adding that any interest rate changes needed to be “very measured”.

Will Christine Lagarde take a shot at the French presidency?

During the early days of the Greek sovereign debt crisis in 2011 and 2012, Knot made headlines by becoming one of the first officials to publicly discuss whether the country might default on its debts or might leave the euro, warning it must not happen involuntarily.

He said his intention was not to argue in favour of such drastic steps but to warn about a “disorderly default or an involuntary Greek exit” as both would have had “devastating effects” on financial stability in Greece and the rest of Europe.

In September 2019, Knot caused a stir by issuing a rare public rebuke of a decision by the ECB’s governing council, when Draghi had pushed through a controversial restart of bond buying and a further reduction in negative interest rates.

“My main concern was about proportionality at a time when the side effects [of quantitative easing] were clearly accumulating,” he said, adding that he preferred to make his point in public rather than have it emerge anonymously through media reports.

“The bar for publishing such a statement again today would clearly be higher,” he acknowledged. – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

Adjusted Ebitda in this division rose 6 per cent in the quarter to $28.7 million due to improved banana pricing in North America and higher banana volumes in Europe, but the pricing and sales benefits were partially offset by elevated pineapple production costs due to adverse weather conditions.

Dole’s diversified fresh produce business in Europe increased its revenue by 9.3 per cent to $1.09 billion in the third quarter, but adjusted Ebitda fell by 3.1 per cent to $39.4 million due to weaker performance in the Netherlands and Spain.

Revenue also rose at its diversified fresh produce operation in the Americas, with sales up 14.1 per cent to $479.2 million as a result of higher volumes in key products, including kiwis, avocados, grapes and tomatoes. Adjusted Ebitda also rose 22.8 per cent to $15.8 million.

]]><![CDATA[Profits jump 13% to €7.5m at gift card group One4All ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/09/profits-jump-13-to-75m-at-gift-card-group-one4all/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/09/profits-jump-13-to-75m-at-gift-card-group-one4all/Mon, 09 Nov 2026 14:28:14 +0000Pretax profits at the company that sells One4All gift cards in Ireland jumped by 13 per cent to €7.54 million last year.

The principal activities of the business are the sale of gift cards – both physical and digital – that can be used at a wide range of stores in Ireland and online. The company sells the vouchers directly and also through a number of distribution partners, including Tesco, An Post and Dealz.

Accounts filed by GVS Gift Voucher Shop DAC show profits were running ahead of the 7.5 per cent growth in revenue to €29.79 million in the year to the end of January 3rd this year.

The GVS business generates funds from its inactive balance charge where a inactive balance charge of €1.45 which is levied on each card every months from 19 months after it is issued. The charge continues until the balance on the card is zero.

A geographical breakdown of the TSC group’s revenues show that €30.42 million, or roughly a third of the €92 million in total revenue, was generated in Ireland in 2025.

Last year, the Irish business paid a €30 million dividend to TSC Ventures DAC which, in turn, paid the €30 million to its shareholders.

GVS Gift Voucher Shop’s directors say they are satisfied with the performance of the company “and are confident that sufficient appropriate systems and controls are in place to ensure future turnover and profit growth”.

The business recorded a profit after tax of €6.53 million, once a €1 million corporation tax charge is accounted for.

A separate entity owned by TSC Ventures, GVS Prepaid (Europe) Ltd, is responsible for the management and safeguarding of Irish client funds held in One4All gift vouchers.

At the end of 2025, the value of unredeemed balances on One4All gift cards in Ireland was €201.9 million which was held in a special client bank account. The company generated €1.25 million in interest income during 2025.

Numbers employed at GVS Gift Voucher Shop dipped last year by seven to 53 but staff costs rose marginally from €2.98 million to €3.09 million.

GVS Gift Voucher Shop GVS Prepaid (Europe) and TSC Ventures are all ultimately owned by US company Blackhawk Network Holdings. The California-headquartered fintech acquired GVS from shareholders that included State-owned An Post in a €100 million deal in 2018.

]]>RuslanDashinsky<![CDATA[AI agents in car dealerships: No time off and they work out how quickly a vehicle will sell]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/09/ai-agents-in-car-dealerships-they-never-take-time-off-or-get-sick-and-can-work-out-how-quickly-vehicles-will-sell/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/09/ai-agents-in-car-dealerships-they-never-take-time-off-or-get-sick-and-can-work-out-how-quickly-vehicles-will-sell/Mon, 09 Nov 2026 05:47:00 +0000Car sales, to the buyer at least, haven’t changed all that much since Henry Ford first rolled out the Model T. The sector is long established, with many dealerships in Ireland having decades of heritage.

It’s a human business. One that involves talking to customers, assessing vehicles, deciding what stock to buy and avoid, and, of course, closing sales. On the face of it, this is hardly the poster child for disruption by artificial intelligence (AI).

Yet AI is making an impact, with several Irish companies at the forefront of that movement, with Irish dealers embracing the time benefits that come with deploying AI agents.

“It’s an age-old problem. Leads aren’t responded to quickly enough and they’re not followed up regularly enough,” says Shaun Donnellan, founder of AutoAgent, a company that develops AI agents for dealerships. “Dealerships are too busy, salespeople have huge amounts of paperwork and prep to do along with getting cars from A to B, and much more.

“AutoAgent helps with a lot of that because it handles the mundane side of selling to the customer. The precious commodity for customers is time. When I started selling cars in 2012, they had far more time to come in and do things. Today, people have so little time that they visit less than two dealerships per purchase on average.”

Speed matters in this sector and anywhere in the process where hours or even minutes can be saved is crucial. By the time a buyer is looking at dealerships to engage with, they’ve usually already narrowed down what they want from Google searches.

For the dealership, the goal is to capture and keep the buyer’s attention while their interest is at its peak.

“The customer wants the car. There are probably a few versions of the car available. The first person that responds and captures their time will most likely bring them in and sell them the car,” he says.

Donnellan has already worked with Tony Burke Motors to roll out his AI agents, with the agent having a direct impact on sales.

The long road to building an Irish AI start-up

“Tony has already been a leader for technology in the sector. When I came to him with this, he leaned into it hard. It booked nine appointments for his dealership in July, with five of those turning into sales,” says Donnellan.

AutoAgent deployed Aran, its bespoke agent, with Tony Burke Motors to engage with customers when humans weren’t on hand.

“It’s a response optimisation platform that responds to customers and captures their interest while it’s at its peak. It never takes time off, is never sick, and responds the way your dealership wants with your process,” he says.

What Donnellan is doing is reflecting the wider benefit of AI agents to the auto dealership sector, according to Muireann Heaney, an AI engineer with AI One.

“If you look at a company like AutoAgent, they’ve identified the point in the sales cycle of where issues come up. What they’ve done is realise the information is there and focus on keeping the customer interested for the dealerships,” says Heaney.

“With dealerships, getting the engagement from customers at the start is critical for them. That way the customer knows the dealership is interested and wants to give them information that can help their buying decision.”

Would you trust this AI to sell you a second-hand car?

There is, however, the old adage of more haste, less speed. A classic misuse of AI is getting the fastest answer possible rather than the best one.

“Speed isn’t the major concern because a normal consumer is willing to wait a few seconds. They are focused mostly on accurate and relevant information that they can verify. A fast answer doesn’t always mean it’s a good answer,” says Janet Xiu Shi, an AI quality evaluation adviser.

Of course, trial runs and small roll-outs are one thing. Once AI use goes into full usage within any business, somebody has to be in charge of what it is and isn’t permitted to do. The car dealership sector is no exception.

“From a business perspective, leadership needs to know how to measure AI effectiveness and who takes accountability for it. Operationally, the team needs to know what AI is and isn’t allowed to use as well as being able to evaluate its output,” says Xiu Shi.

That’s why companies like TradeBid have embraced a hybrid approach. The company uses AI to help assess trade-ins but also knows that mistakes can be made. Low-confidence cases automatically get escalated to be looked over by human eyes.

“On the inspection side, because our business relies on the accuracy of AI, we have to make sure the information is as good as possible. Where the confidence is too low on the AI side, we bring in people to take a look,” says Conor O’Boyle, co-founder of TradeBid.

Peter Thiel-backed AI company Cognition establishes Irish presence

The value goes beyond the individual sale to the broader decisions that a dealership wants to make. AI’s value goes beyond customer service work – indeed, quite a lot of it isn’t customer facing at all. It can aid dealerships working out what vehicles to acquire and how quickly they will sell.

“Dealers often complain to us that they don’t have enough time to know what they should be buying. We have so much data that we take retail feeds and analyse it to provide dealers with more discoverability so they can turn over cars faster.”

Time remains at the heart of the problem for dealerships wherever you look. It’s why James Flynn’s Coso.ai is working with them to free that up. His business uses AI to reduce the time spent by businesses on social media.

“Creating content takes a lot of time. Beyond just writing, you’re creating images, graphic design, video editing and more. A week’s worth of content for a business usually takes half a day’s work for them. We cut that down to 15 or 20 minutes on a Friday morning,” says O’Flynn.

That time on a Friday morning, or whatever day, is crucial to a service like Coso.ai working, he says.

“Where you need to watch out is that you don’t necessarily want a full autopilot, because it’s AI, but you want it specific to your brand,” he says.

“Around 90 per cent of businesses don’t have a dedicated social media marketer. We do that element to free up time for people. We’re not putting anyone out of a job, we’re taking a functionality that previously only existed in large companies and putting it into the hands of small and medium businesses across the country.”

The biggest advocates for AI in industry have long cried out that AI will assist workers rather than replace them. A sector as human-centric as car sales might well be the best use-case for those advocates.

Where the disruption is happening is centred around freeing up time for those working in the industry to focus on what they do best, and deliver the most value to the sector.

“AI agents allow the humans in the company to go back to what they are good at. It means they can meet more people in person per day because they have that first step taken care of,” says Heaney.

“The key thing is operational leverage. Nobody wants AI all the time, we like human interaction, but automating the parts of your business that are repeatable operations is where we’ll see the biggest difference.”

]]>Jose Ignacio Martin Del Barco<![CDATA[Kingspan forecasts spike in 2026 trading profit as data centre sales surge]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/09/kingspan-forecasts-spike-in-2026-trading-profit-as-data-centre-sales-surge/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/09/kingspan-forecasts-spike-in-2026-trading-profit-as-data-centre-sales-surge/Mon, 09 Nov 2026 11:03:07 +0000Sales at building materials group Kingspan rose 10 per cent to €7.6 billion in the first nine months of the year, the company said in a trading update on Monday.

The Cavan-based multinational, led by Gene Murtagh, said third quarter sales rose 16 per cent year on year, mainly due to underlying sales growth of 12 per cent.

In the update, the company has forecast it will deliver a full-year trading profit in the region of €1.15 billion, which would mark an improvement of 20 per cent on last year’s performance.

Kingspan added the company’s strong backlog and pipeline would likely lead to trading profits in the region of €1.47 billion next year – growth of almost 28 per cent – “assuming our end-markets remain relatively stable”.

“Whilst end-markets have their obvious challenges, the global backlog is ahead year on year,” the company said.

Further details in the trading update showed Kingspan’s insulated building envelopes sales rose by 4 per cent in the first nine months and by 8 per cent in the third quarter.

“As ever, there is considerable variability in sector and territory performances with our vast array of addressable applications around the world contributing positively overall,” Kingspan’s statement said.

The company said its majority non-residential end-market exposure was “relatively stable overall”, while residential markets remained subdued for the most part.

It added the pace of activity in the Americas region had picked up since midyear and performance in continental Europe had been “positive overall”, with activity softer in France in recent months, and the Middle East market “resilient”.

Kingspan’s unit Advnsys, which is focused on supplying an international data centre boom with bespoke critical infrastructure, recorded a 41 per cent increase in sales in the first nine months of the year, with third quarter sales up 54 per cent year-on-year.

The company said its order intake reached €2.7 billion in the year-to-date to the end of September, more than double that of the same period last year.

“We are experiencing an ever-increasing wave of inbound inquiries and continue to roll out capacity and associated supply chain resilience as rapidly as possible to meet demand,” the company said.

It added that activity at a new production facility in Arkansas “has ramped up considerably” and a new facility in Kentucky entered production in June. Kingspan has plans for further developments, in Europe, Southeast Asia and Latin America, some of which are already under way with others still at the planning stage.

In August, Kingspan announced the acquisition of BMC Manufacturing Group, a data centre-focused group, in a landmark deal worth up to €900 million. Kingspan’s trading update said the deal was completed at the end of September and it has begun integration of the business into the group.

]]>Naoise Culhane<![CDATA[Housing guide delayed as workers worry about pensions]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/09/housing-guide-delayed-as-workers-worry-about-pensions/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/09/housing-guide-delayed-as-workers-worry-about-pensions/Mon, 09 Nov 2026 06:39:38 +0000More than two years after the Department of Housing introduced guidelines to support new forms of compact residential developments in Ireland, home builders and planners are still waiting for a playbook for applying the new measures.

The guidelines were put in place to help developers deliver own-door homes on sites where apartments are deemed unviable. The Department said a design manual detailing best practice, promised for early 2024, was still incomplete.

Many workers in Ireland are concerned their pensions will not be big enough for a comfortable retirement, according to a new report from AIB.

Dominic Coyle reports that despite the clear anxiety demonstrated among workers, more than six in 10 have never reviewed their pension arrangements with an adviser.

AI is reshaping many industries and work practices, and it appears even the car dealerships, where the human touch is deemed so crucial to a sale, are not immune.

Several Irish firms have built AI agents for showrooms that help them follow up on enquiries, book appointments, assess trade-ins and create social media content, which has freed up staff to spend more time with customers, writes Emmet Ryan.

In his latest weekly economics column, Prof John FitzGerald discusses the reliance of Ireland’s economy on migrant workers from outside the EU to address skills shortages.

He argues that cutting work permits, especially for those providing care to the country’s ageing population, would lead to a big headache for the State as the sector struggle without immigrant nurses from countries such as the Philippines.

In her weekly column, Pilita Clark considers a question that may unsettle people managers. As AI agents take on more workplace tasks, managers could end up overseeing fewer people and more bots.

Considering managerial salaries have long been tied to the size of their workforce, she asks whether managers should be paid less if they were responsible for a group of AI agents rather than human staff.

In Monday’s edition, we also have a piece from Frank Rubotham, head of specialists and propositions at Logicalis UK and Ireland, who is writing about ComReg’s proposed licensing framework for private 5G networks.

He writes it could help Irish businesses modernise and attract investment in sectors such as pharma, advanced manufacturing and logistics.

If you’d like to read more about the issues that affect your finances, try signing up to On the Money, the weekly newsletter from our personal finance team, which will be issued every Friday to Irish Times subscribers.

   <description>Der britische Schauspieler, Comedian und Kinderbuchautor David Walliams – bekannt etwa aus „Little Britain“ – sieht sich mit Vorwürfen sexuellen Fehlverhaltens gegenüber mehreren jungen Frauen und Mädchen konfrontiert. Poland has detained and charged two Ukrainian citizens accused of carrying out espionage and acts of sabotage on behalf of Russia.

The men, aged 24 and 25, were allegedly paid to conduct reconnaissance of critical infrastructure and military facilities across Poland. They are also accused of setting fire to several vehicles with the aim of stoking anti-Ukrainian sentiment.

Funkcjonariusze Agencji Bezpieczeństwa Wewnętrznego zatrzymali w Mińsku Mazowieckim dwóch obywateli Ukrainy w wieku 24 i 25 lat podejrzanych o szpiegostwo i prowadzenie działań dywersyjnych na zlecenie rosyjskich służb specjalnych.
▶️ Mężczyźni rozpoznawali i robili zdjęcia… pic.twitter.com/G3i8hEsBHT

— Tomasz Siemoniak (@TomaszSiemoniak) November 10, 2026

The suspects were detained by Poland’s Internal Security Agency (ABW) on 3 November in Mińsk Mazowiecki, a town just outside Warsaw, the capital. ABW officers also searched their residences and other locations connected to the investigation, seizing data storage devices and narcotics.

According to investigators, the suspects were tasked with setting vehicles on fire after changing their licence plates to ones used by Ukrainian military vehicles. This was “aimed at fueling anti-Ukrainian sentiment”, says the National Prosecutor’s Office.

Prosecutors have charged the men under Poland’s espionage law with working against Poland on behalf of a foreign intelligence service – a crime that carries a minimum prison sentence of five years – and sabotage on behalf of foreign intelligence, which is punishable by 10 years to life.

At the prosecutor’s request, a court ordered both suspects to be placed in pretrial detention for three months.

 

In recent years, Poland has seen a huge rise in cases of espionage and sabotage carried out on behalf of Russia.

The ABW launched 48 investigations related to espionage last year, more than twice as many as in 2024. In those two years taken together, there were more espionage investigations than over the previous three decades combined.

Earlier this year, the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism published a report identifying Poland as the “primary focus” of Russia’s campaign of sabotage in Europe.

Four men – three Ukrainians and a Belarusian – have gone on trial in Warsaw accused of being part of a criminal group that carried out a series of arson attacks in Poland and Lithuania on behalf of Russia https://t.co/i4czRb9DYZ

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 12, 2026

Last month, a Polish man was jailed for five and a half years for spying on behalf of Russia. The tasks assigned to him included reconnaissance of an airport as part of a possible plan to assassinate Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky while he travelled through Poland.

Shortly afterwards, the trial began of four men – three Ukrainians and one Belarusian – accused of being part of a criminal group that carried out a series of arson attacks in Poland and Lithuania on Russian orders.

In July, a Russian married couple with refugee status in Poland were convicted of working as spies on behalf of Moscow. In October, a member of Poland’s military reserve, who holds both Polish and Ukrainian citizenship, was detained on suspicion of espionage.

By Aleks Szczerbiak

Poland’s escalating Constitutional Tribunal (TK) dispute is no longer simply a legal argument about contested appointments but a struggle over who defines constitutional legitimacy.

As the liberal-centrist government and right-wing opposition and president advance rival rule-of-law claims, the conflict risks entrenching a system of legal dualism in which judicial authority depends on political allegiance rather than broad constitutional consent.

The roots of the crisis

Poland’s 15-member TK is a powerful body that rules on the constitutionality of the country’s laws. The roots of the current dispute trace back to late 2015 and began immediately prior to the right-wing Law and Justice (PiS) party taking office following its October parliamentary election victory.

In its final weeks in power, the outgoing government, led by the liberal-centrist Civic Platform (PO, now Civic Coalition: KO), fast-tracked the appointment of five tribunal members who were replacing those whose terms were set to expire in November and December.

Upon winning an outright parliamentary majority, the incoming PiS-led government refused to recognise these appointments, elected a slate of five new tribunal members, and party-backed President Andrzej Duda swore them in.

Fifteen months since the change of government, Poland's rule-of-law crisis continues – indeed, many Poles think the situation has got worse.@J_Jaraczewski explains the roots of the crisis, what its impact has been, and how it might be resolved https://t.co/7KOCURV3dU

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 17, 2025

The tribunal (still largely composed of pre-2015 judges) ruled that three of the outgoing parliament’s appointments were lawful, so only two of the new ones could stand. PiS refused to accept this, creating the so-called “understudy” judges (dublerzy) controversy.

As further vacancies arose, the new parliament gradually installed its nominees, culminating in the appointment at the end of 2016 of one of them, Julia Przyłębska, as tribunal president. Przyłębska’s leadership was contested on procedural grounds, as was that of her 2024 successor Bogdan Święczkowski, a former senior prosecutor closely aligned with the 2015-23 PiS administration.

All of this led to the then-opposition parties and much of the Polish legal and the EU political establishments denouncing the tribunal as legally compromised and politically captured.

Total non-cooperation

Following the autumn 2023 parliamentary election, a new coalition government headed up by KO leader Donald Tusk embraced a policy of total non-cooperation with the tribunal, refusing to publish its rulings.

The battle for control took a new turn when, after initially not filling any tribunal vacancies, from March 2026 onwards the new parliament elected successive waves of new members, reaching eight by September.

However, PiS-aligned President Karol Nawrocki (who succeeded Duda in August 2025) refused to swear in five of these nominees, including former minister and close Tusk ally Maciej Berek. In response, the government took the unprecedented step of swearing in the contested nominees directly in parliament, a move that both Nawrocki and Święczkowski rejected as illegal.

The standoff between the government and president over Poland’s constitutional court deepened today, as Maciej Berek, whom the prime minister recently described as his “right-hand man”, took his oath as a new judge without the presence of the president https://t.co/MrExiJRsEN

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 14, 2026

The conflict escalated sharply at the end of last month, when, backed by the government and tribunal members elected by the current parliamentary majority, Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, one of the five contested nominees but having the longest judicial tenure, asserted her seniority to order a one-month suspension of Święczkowski and his deputy Bartłomiej Sochański in their official duties and assumed temporary control.

Justice minister Waldemar Żurek submitted requests to lift Święczkowski and Sochański’s immunity as the newly appointed members, and the new nominees entered the tribunal building under State Protection Service (UOP) escort.

This triggered protests by right-wing opposition supporters at the building’s gates, prompting a heavy police presence and tense stand-off. The severity of this was underscored when Nawrocki cut short an official visit to Senegal mid-flight, returned to Warsaw and entered the tribunal building in the early hours, condemning what he described as a violation of the constitutional order.

During a visit to the Constitutional Tribunal last night, President Nawrocki clashed physically and verbally with judges involved in an attempt to take control of the court.

The president is today seeking talks with political leaders to discuss the crisis https://t.co/7HmBnuIaDG

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 31, 2026

Korwin-Piotrowska then convened a tribunal general assembly which critics argued lacked the legally required two-thirds quorum because only eight of its 15 nominal members (the newly elected ones, including the five who had not taken the presidential oath) attended.

Her supporters maintained that the quorum was met because the suspension of Święczkowski and Sochański, and exclusion of the last remaining “understudy” judge, reduced the pool of eligible members to 12.

The government’s “transitional justice” logic

For the Tusk government and its legal defenders, these exceptional executive and parliamentary countermeasures were framed through the logic of “transitional justice”: as painful and extraordinary but necessary to restore the rule of law after PiS had violated the constitution and European standards, systematically packing the tribunal with political loyalists.

Justifying its non-recognition of tribunal rulings, the government argued that the presence of three defectively elected “understudy” members and their successors, together with Przyłębska’s and Święczkowski’s procedurally flawed presidential appointments, fundamentally “contaminated” the entire body, thereby invalidating its rulings.

In its efforts to restore democracy, the government may sometimes take actions that are “not fully compliant with the law”, admits @donaldtusk.

But he says this is because of the legal chaos deliberately created by the former PiS government https://t.co/AWlM6hRLie

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 11, 2024

To provide what it argued was authoritative external confirmation of this defect, the government relied heavily on landmark European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) and EU Court of Justice (CJEU) rulings which determined that, thus constituted, the tribunal could no longer be considered a legitimate body established by legal standards.

From this perspective, refusing to recognise the tribunal’s allegedly unlawful rulings was framed as the only available mechanism to neutralise a partisan weapon that PiS had left behind to block the government’s legislative agenda.

Alternative parliamentary swearing-in procedures were justified on the grounds that the president’s role in receiving oaths was purely ceremonial, not a constitutionally mandated requirement.

 

Despite his recent political role, Berek’s appointment was defended on the basis that he played more of a technocratic-expert role within the government, and was highly qualified to undertake the extraordinary transitional measures required to repair a damaged institution.

Defenders of the tribunal leadership’s suspension and occupation of its headquarters argued that by blocking the new nominees from taking up their roles, Święczkowski had paralysed the institution and decisive measures were necessary to restore its proper functioning.

A “coup d’état”?

PiS and Nawrocki, on the other hand, maintained that the Tusk government’s actions amounted to an authoritarian attempt to operate completely outside of constitutional powers, treating legality as an option when it conflicted with its political agenda.

They insisted that all of its 2015 appointments were in full accordance with the law, correcting an improper attempt by the outgoing PO-dominated parliament to entrench its influence after electoral defeat, and that the tribunal’s ruling on the legality of these three “understudy” judges went beyond its jurisdiction.

Successive tribunal general assemblies, they argued, validly and legally selected Przyłębska and then Święczkowski as presidents, and the Tusk government had no constitutional right to pick and choose which tribunal rulings it would recognise. They said that, by delaying the election of some new members when vacancies arose, the government violated existing procedures.

The constitution, they said, explicitly required these new nominees to take their oaths directly “before the president” and that by conducting improper parliamentary swearing-in ceremonies they had effectively renounced their offices.

The International Commission of Jurists has criticised the takeover of Poland’s constitutional court, saying it “contravenes international standards on the independence of the judiciary”

But it also criticised the president for refusing to swear in judges https://t.co/2kBv3GT20d

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 4, 2026

The candidacy of Berek, a recently active politician with doubtful professional qualifications, they said represented its own form of institutional capture and selective legality.

The suspension of the tribunal leadership and occupation of its headquarters amounted to an unlawful power grab or “coup d’état” that completely disregarded established constitutional procedures.

PiS rejected the “contamination” thesis and argued vigorously that Poland had never transferred jurisdiction over the organisation of the national judiciary to EU institutions and European courts, who had no authority to evaluate the legality of tribunal appointments.

They accused the EU political establishment of double standards, weaponising “rule-of-law” arguments to help a politically aligned government while ignoring the Tusk administration’s own executive overreach.

PiS also argued that by delegitimising a tribunal which had in the past ruled that the Polish Constitution superseded EU law, the Tusk government was paving the way for controversial social and economic policies to be pushed through without any domestic judicial oversight.

Tusk’s liberal critics

On the other hand, more ideologically supportive liberal critics of the Tusk government’s approach acknowledged the original 2015 irregularities but warned that selective non-recognition of an entire institution, combined with attempts to install a new tribunal without presidential participation, risked creating the same dual legitimacy problem that they accused PiS of having started.

They stressed that lasting repair required broad political consensus and careful adherence to formal procedures so that future majorities did not simply invert the non-recognition tactic. They noted the tension with earlier condemnations of PiS for elevating politically aligned figures or recently active politicians.

While sympathetic to the goal of reforming what they believed was a deeply compromised tribunal, these critics argued that, by employing legally questionable shortcuts and executive force, the Tusk government risked setting dangerous precedents and deepening the very disorder that it was claiming to correct.

Interestingly, the government’s broader “transitional justice” justificatory logic – that ordinary procedures would not adequately address a systemic capture and the priority had to be functional restoration rather than abstract purity – mirrored the arguments PiS itself advanced for its own judicial reforms after 2015.

The right-wing party argued that the post-1989 judiciary remained dominated by a post-communist elite that required deep structural overhaul rather than incremental change.

A high-risk escalation

The latest escalation is likely to entrench and intensify the profound systemic polarisation that characterises the Polish political scene, for a long-time embodied in the KO-PiS duopoly, with the conflict framed in existential terms of either “restoring the rule of law” or “defending the constitutional order”.

This fierce dispute lies at the heart of the Tusk government’s broader political “reckoning” (rozliczenie) agenda involving visibly removing PiS’s influence from key institutions.

For the ruling coalition, this was a central 2023 election campaign message, and being seen to deliver on it is an absolute political necessity to satisfy and mobilise its electoral base. A confrontational approach thus serves to consolidate the government’s support among these core voters, who have grown increasingly impatient and want to see decisive action.

However, the government’s strategy is fraught with political risk. High-stakes tactics risk uniting its right-wing opponents and alienating moderate voters increasingly exhausted by endless, hyper-partisan institutional confrontation, legal brinkmanship and the optics of police deployments around a key state body.

They provide the president and right-wing opposition with a powerful counternarrative of constitutional vandalism ahead of the next parliamentary election.

Escalation is also straining relations within the ruling coalition, especially among more conservative or legalistic coalition partners who believe that a more fundamental constitutional “reset” based on a cross-party settlement is required to break the impasse in the longer term.

The leader of one of the parties in Poland’s ruling coalition has proposed a “constitutional reset” to resolve the crisis around the country’s top court.

It would involve removing all current judges and choosing new ones in a more consensual process https://t.co/xDwpRUVHxG

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 6, 2026

Internationally, although the EU political establishment remains supportive of the Tusk government’s actions, they invite uneasy scrutiny of the stability of Poland’s legal system and have drawn explicit criticism from the US embassy.

The reliance on a “transitional justice” framing that echoes PiS’s earlier justifications for systemic change, combined with the appointment to the tribunal of a recent minister despite prior criticisms of politicised nominations, also undercuts government claims of consistent principle and provides the right with a powerful narrative of hypocrisy.

Legal dualism

Ultimately, this bitter dispute has paved the way for a protracted and deeply destabilising “legal dualism” that could plague the Polish state for years to come, with a tribunal simultaneously legitimate and illegitimate depending on who holds power.

By treating the tribunal as an illegitimate entity when its nominees did not control it, the current government has established a precedent.

Even if it now appears to have secured a clear majority for its own nominees, a future right-wing government and sympathetic president will have every incentive to use the exact same playbook: treating the reconstituted tribunal as a captured instrument of the liberal establishment, and regarding it as no more legitimate than the Tusk government did the PiS-era one.

Consequently, the tribunal’s authority, and legal certainty in Poland more generally, have been further eroded, leaving the country without a widely accepted arbiter to resolve constitutional disputes. There are no immediate prospects for a durable resolution of this conflict.

Thousands of soldiers from 11 countries began military exercises in Poland today. They are the first organised by the so-called Coalition of the Willing, with the aim of preparing for a role in supporting Ukraine following a potential future peace deal with Russia.

The manoeuvres, which are being jointly led by France and the UK, are taking place in Nowa Dęba, around 100 kilometres from the Ukrainian border, and will last until 22 November.

The development has been condemned by Russia, which says it shows that Western countries are ignoring Moscow’s “legitimate security concerns” and “fueling the spiral of escalation”.​

The plans were first announced in July by Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk following a summit of the Coalition of the Willing in Paris. The exercises, taking place on land, in the air, and at sea, are being conducted by the Multinational Force Ukraine (MNF-U), which serves as the military component of the coalition.

“This exercise will show that the Multinational Force-Ukraine is a real, capable, readily deployable force that represents a serious commitment from Coalition of the Willing nations to Ukraine’s long-term stability and security,” said Tom Bateman, the British lieutenant-general commanding MNF-U.

The British Ministry of Defence says that the exercise, which has been named “Koalicja” (meaning “Coalition” in Polish), “will test Allies’ readiness to support Ukraine and rebuild their Armed Forces once the conflict ends”.

France’s armed forces ministry, meanwhile, says that the aim is to ensure that MNF-U is “ready to deploy at the request of the Ukrainian government” in order to help “guarantee a robust and lasting peace in Ukraine”.

 

Around 2,800 troops are being deployed for the manoeuvres, with AFP reporting that this includes 1,100 from France alone. The British defence ministry says it has sent 300 personnel, as well as Typhoon and Voyager aircraft.

In addition, just under 2,000 Polish troops will take part, bringing the total to almost 5,000 personnel, reports Polska Zbrojna, a publication linked to the Polish defence ministry. Other countries taking part are Belgium, Estonia, Germany, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Spain, Sweden and Turkey.

Poland’s defence ministry says the exercises will “demonstrate how quickly participating nations can mobilise and establish forces capable of supporting Ukraine after the end of the war”.

However, although Poland is hosting the manoeuvres, the defence ministry reiterated the country’s position that “it would not send its own soldiers to Ukrainian territory” as part of any postwar settlement. Poland has made clear it intends instead to help provide logistical support.

In the wake of Saturday’s deadly terrorist shooting in Kraków, a deputy defence minister has called for debate on limiting the number and types of weapons people can own. Meanwhile, a deputy interior minister says the tragedy provides an “incentive” to revisit proposals to better register certain guns.

Poland has among the lowest levels of gun ownership in Europe, though the number of firearms licences being issued has risen in recent years and some politicians have called for expanded access to guns. Saturday’s attack was carried out by a man who legally owned firearms.

On Saturday, 24-year-old Michał Oksiński drove through the historic city centre of Kraków, which was packed with tourists and locals, firing at random from his car.

He killed six people and injured over a dozen more. Later in the day, the bodies of the perpetrator’s parents and sister were found in his home, where they had been shot dead.

Oksiński’s rampage was brought to an end in a shootout with two police officers, which left all three with serious injuries. On Monday morning, the police announced that Oksiński had died in hospital. One of the police officers remains in what is described as “serious but stable” condition.

She added that “it’s already relatively easy” to obtain a gun licence, which can be granted to anyone aged 21 or over who has passed the relevant tests and declared that the firearm is for sporting purposes. Both Oksiński and his father had such licences and legally owned 11 firearms.

Last year’s deficit, at 7.3% of GDP, was the second-highest in the European Union. This year it is forecast to drop slightly, to 6.7%, according to recent finance ministry projections. But next year’s budget foresees a deficit of 7.1%.

Those figures are much higher than those the government pledged to reach when, in 2024, Poland was placed under the EU’s excessive deficit procedure. For example, the deficit was supposed to fall to 3.7% of GDP in 2027.

Moody’s, one of the big three global credit rating agencies, has cut Poland’s rating from A2 to A3.

The last time the agency had Poland at such a low level was 2002. It is also the first time any of the big three agencies has downgraded Poland since 2016 https://t.co/qUAEouqhlx

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 19, 2026

S&P says that it projects Poland’s net debt exceeding 70% of GDP by 2029. That rise of “more than 20 percentage points over five years marks one of the most significant fiscal deteriorations globally”.

The agency notes that Poland will hold parliamentary elections in 2027, making any “meaningful consolidation unlikely” before then. Moreover, the veto power of opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki means the government “faces constraints in advancing its legislative and fiscal consolidation agenda”.

Pointing to the ongoing crisis around the constitutional court, S&P also warns that “renewed institutional tensions could weigh on policy predictability”.

However, the agency notes that Poland’s economy remains “resilient”, with real GDP growth projected to average around 3% between 2027 and 2029. It also points to the fact that the country has seen a peak in EU-funded investment this year, while exports have picked up.

 

As well as shifting Poland’s overall outlook to negative, S&P downgraded its local currency ratings – meaning its assessment of the country’s willingness and ability to service debt denominated in domestic currency – from A/A-1 to A-/A-2, the same level as its foreign currency ratings.

“Our fiscal projections are now weaker than previously envisaged, and we note a track record of recent fiscal slippages amid a challenging policy environment, which underpin our assessment of Poland’s reduced fiscal flexibility,” wrote the agency.

Finance minister Andrzej Domański acknowledged S&P’s decision to lower Poland’s outlook to negative in a social media post. However, he pointed to the section of the agency’s report in which it said that the government is constrained by presidential vetoes.

Nawrocki has vetoed a record number of bills since becoming president last year, including several fiscal measures. “Despite the presidential vetoes, we will continue taking steps to strengthen the country’s finances,” wrote Domański.

🇵🇱 Agencja S&P utrzymała rating Polski na poziomie A-, obniżając jednak jego perspektywę do negatywnej.

W uzasadnieniu decyzji czytamy wprost:

„Rząd premiera Donalda Tuska napotyka ograniczenia w realizacji swoich planów legislacyjnych i konsolidacji finansów publicznych ze…

— Andrzej Domański (@Domanski_Andrz) November 6, 2026

However, Nawrocki notes that the ballooning budget deficits preceded his coming to power, and has blamed the government of Prime Minister Donald Tusk for overseeing budgetary “chaos” and causing “a deep crisis of credibility”.

In response to S&P’s announcement, Marcin Ociepa, deputy head of the parliamentary caucus of Law and Justice (PiS), the largest opposition party, accused the government of “trying to shift responsibility for Poland’s credit rating downgrade [sic] onto the president”.

“Any family that managed its finances the way Donald Tusk manages our country’s finances would drown in debt and go bankrupt,” wrote Ociepa. “That is exactly what awaits Poland if this government remains in power.”

A collection of artefacts associated with the Vandals and dating back almost 2,000 years has been handed anonymously to a museum in eastern Poland.

The collection includes a sword, spear and javelin heads, shield components and spurs. Museum staff do not know who originally discovered the burial or exactly where it was located, leaving the circumstances of the find largely a mystery.

The Father Stanisław Staszic Museum in Hrubieszów announced in a Facebook post that the objects had been passed to them anonymously through an intermediary.

The items are in poor condition and will undergo urgent conservation, with the iron components of the weapons particularly vulnerable after centuries in the ground.

They were also exposed to high temperatures during a burial practice in which the deceased was burned along with their personal belongings. The museum says that the nature of the objects indicates that their owner held a high social position.

The most notable object is a sword preserved in three pieces, reflecting the Vandal practice of deliberately breaking or bending weapons and other grave artefacts as part of funeral rituals. The collection also contains two spearheads, both broken.

Other items include a shield boss with a spike, a shield grip, a fragment of a knife, a belt buckle and two spurs. Fragments of a bone comb and a bronze fibula, used to fasten a cloak, were also recovered.

 

The circumstances surrounding the discovery and recovery of the objects remain unknown, but the museum says that, according to the information it has received, the burial site was discovered in an agricultural field several years ago in the municipality of Werbkowice.

“We intend to verify the exact location through archaeological excavations, most likely next summer,” they added. “Based on the information we have gathered, there are strong indications that there may be more similar burials in the area that have been disturbed by agricultural work.”

The opportunity to recover the objects and transfer them to an appropriate institution arose only recently. The museum said that a local metal detectorist played a key role in arranging the transfer, acting as an intermediary in securing the artefacts.

The recovery of the artefacts follows another recent archaeological discovery in the same region. In August, the museum announced that a metal boss from a warrior’s shield dating to the second century was found at a scrap metal yard near Hrubieszów.

The Vandals were an ancient Germanic people believed to have reached the territories of present-day Poland around the 3rd or 2nd century BC.

They lived in the region for several centuries and are generally associated by researchers with the Przeworsk culture, which flourished across parts of present-day Poland during the Iron Age and Roman period.

Around the turn of the 4th and 5th centuries AD, amid the expansion of the Huns, they left Central Europe and moved westwards into the declining Roman Empire. As the Vandals left Central Europe, the Slavic population gradually moved into the region over the following centuries.

The leader of one of the parties in Poland’s ruling coalition has put forward plans for a “constitutional reset” that he hopes can resolve the crisis around the country’s top court.

The proposal, presented on Thursday by deputy prime minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, head of the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), would remove all current judges on the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) and allow new judges to be chosen only with the approval of 60% of members of parliament and the president.

To take effect, the measure would require amending Poland’s constitution, something that has happened only twice since the document was adopted in 1997 and which also requires a three-fifths majority in the Sejm, the lower house of parliament.

Apelują o to przedstawiciele organizacji społecznych, Rada Przedsiębiorców, Naczelna Rada Adwokacka, Helsińska Fundacja Praw Człowieka i Episkopat Polski.… pic.twitter.com/3RCsKRlSiM

— Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz (@KosiniakKamysz) November 5, 2026

Kosiniak-Kamysz’s announcement comes amid the fallout from events last Friday, when eight new judges elected to the TK this year by the government’s majority in parliament seized control of the court.

They announced that its chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, had been suspended for failing to fulfil his duties, including by refusing to allow most of those judges to take up their seats on the court.

Święczkowski denounced the takeover as an illegal “coup d’état”. He has been backed by the tribunal’s remaining six judges, who, like him, were appointed under the former Law and Justice (PiS) government, which brought the TK under its political influence when it ruled from 2015 to 2023.

 

As well as pitting judges aligned with the national-conservative PiS, which is now the main opposition party, and the current more liberal government against one another, the dispute also centres around the legitimacy of certain judges.

The government points to the fact that PiS unlawfully appointed three judges to the TK in 2015. As a result, both Polish and European courts have found the tribunal in its current form to be illegitimate.

Meanwhile, Poland’s president, Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with PiS, has refused to swear in five of the eight judges appointed by the government’s parliamentary majority this year, citing concerns over how they were chosen or their qualifications.

The International Commission of Jurists has criticised the takeover of Poland’s constitutional court, saying it “contravenes international standards on the independence of the judiciary”

But it also criticised the president for refusing to swear in judges https://t.co/2kBv3GT20d

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 4, 2026

The standoff has led some NGOs and experts to call for a “constitutional reset”, whereby the TK would be reformed to make the process of selecting judges more consensual and less politicised.

Indeed, the current government even proposed legislation in 2024 that would have required new TK judges to be approved by a three-fifths parliamentary majority. The plans would also have removed unlawfully appointed judges from the PiS era and annulled rulings they were involved in.

That prompted the president at the time, Andrzej Duda, who was also aligned with PiS, to send the bills to the TK, which was still packed with PiS-era judges, for assessment. The tribunal rejected them as unconstitutional the following year.

Fifteen months since the change of government, Poland's rule-of-law crisis continues – indeed, many Poles think the situation has got worse.@J_Jaraczewski explains the roots of the crisis, what its impact has been, and how it might be resolved https://t.co/7KOCURV3dU

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 17, 2025

Now, Kosiniak-Kamysz has proposed new legislation intended to resolve the issue. His solution would create a mechanism under which parliament, at the request of the National Council of the Judiciary (KRS), could declare the TK “permanently incapable of performing its duties”.

Such a status could only be declared with the support of a three-fifths majority of both houses of parliament – the Sejm and the Senate – combined. It would have to come at the request of the KRS because, says Kosiniak-Kamysz, the terms of judges cannot be shortened without the participation of other judges.

The process of appointing new TK judges would involve the speaker of the Sejm proposing candidates after obtaining the opinions of the heads of the Supreme Court and the Supreme Administrative Court – which are separate from the TK – as well as professional bodies representing legal professions.

The candidates proposed by the speaker would also have to receive the prior consent of the president. For a new TK judge to be approved, they would have to receive the support of three fifths of members of the Sejm and Senate combined.

💬 336 głosów posłów i senatorów. To wykracza poza większość jakąkolwiek koalicyjną dzisiaj sformułowaną – @KosiniakKamysz w Warszawie pic.twitter.com/iLUuM5TSxQ

— 🍀 PSL (@nowePSL) November 5, 2026

Whereas TK judges currently all serve nine-year terms, under Kosiniak-Kamysz’s proposal, five of the judges would serve three-year terms, five of them six-year terms, and the final five would serve for nine years.

Unlike now, the new judges would not have to swear their oath before the president, but before parliament.

Kosiniak-Kamysz emphasised, however, that the measure was intended as a “one-time” emergency tool. “Later, we will return to the method of selecting judges described today in the constitution, or a better one, if there is a majority for it.”

The current method of choosing new TK judges requires only the support of a majority in the Sejm. However, judges must then swear an oath “before the president”, an issue that has become a bone of contention this year.

The standoff between the government and president over Poland’s constitutional court deepened today, as Maciej Berek, whom the prime minister recently described as his “right-hand man”, took his oath as a new judge without the presence of the president https://t.co/MrExiJRsEN

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 14, 2026

Kosiniak-Kamysz’s plans would require changes to Poland’s constitution, which specifies the manner in which TK judges are chosen. A constitutional amendment requires the support of a three-fifths majority in the Sejm and a simple majority in the Senate. It does not need presidential approval.

PSL itself has only 28 members of the 460-seat Sejm and four senators. Kosiniak-Kamysz acknowledged that “it won’t be an easy road” to win the necessary support for his idea.

He appealed not only to his fellow ruling parties, but also to opposition groups that have expressed their backing for a constitutional reset, such as the centre-right Development Plus (Rozwój Plus) and far-right Confederation (Konfederacja).

On Thursday evening, one of Confederation’s leaders, Sławomir Mentzen, shared a photo of himself meeting Kosiniak-Kamysz, with the caption: “It’s going in the right direction”.

Idzie ku dobremu. pic.twitter.com/zk6lZpi3DL

— Sławomir Mentzen (@SlawomirMentzen) November 5, 2026

However, some voices within the ruling coalition expressed scepticism towards the idea. Borys Budka, a former leader of the centrist Civic Coalition (KO) – which is the largest governing party – said it was “hard to imagine changing the constitution alongside someone like PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński”.

Tomasz Trela of The Left (Lewica) likewise said that, “if anyone thinks The Left will change the constitution arm in arm with PiS, they’re mistaken”, reports Polsat News.

    The traditional professional services model of relying on star ‘rainmaker’ partners has been in the spotlight following the surprising downfall of 95-year-old law firm Weil. But Kroll’s risk advisory president, Brent Tomlinson, firmly believes in building a fluid business on a collaborative culture – and not personalities.

    “We’re not the Big Four, so we don’t have geographical borders, and we don’t have thousands of juniors running around. We are a senior top-heavy platform that is intentionally incentivised to be multi-jurisdictional,” Tomlinson told City AM.

    To offer clients a smoother, faster experience, the risk chief said the New York-headquartered firm’s culture focuses on cross-border collaboration.

    When pitching against competitors, the management consultancy firm highlights its lack of internal silos. “I can point to our competitors when we pitch and say they won’t do that [work across verticals]. We incentivise that way, we’re culturally structured that way, and we are organised that way,” he said.

    But you can’t simply tell people to collaborate, especially in a sector where ‘rainmakers’ are held in high regard. A firm’s commitment to its culture is really tested when money gets involved.

    “The message from the top is clear every day… I [couldn’t] care less if [the revenue] sits in my P&L. [The co-president] couldn’t care less. It does not matter. We are shareholders and leaders first… It does not matter where the revenue goes or who got it, as long as Kroll won,” he said.

    Unsurprisingly, people are happiest collaborating when it leads to winning pitches. “Winning cures everything… people like winning with people they like and who they trust”.

    Firm’s blueprint for growth

    Although headquartered in the US, London is Kroll’s largest office, and around half of its undisclosed revenue comes from outside the US. With growth high on the agenda, Tomlinson, who has been with the firm for over six years, relocated from New York to London two years ago as the office’s first senior executive.

    Tomlinson noted that having dots on a map isn’t enough. Kroll is in 30 countries, across more than 70 offices, but the firm is looking to pivot away from smaller, sub-scale outposts to double down on building out “full suite” capabilities in major financial hubs. “We need more scale in key financial hubs and geographies,” he added.

    On recruitment, the firm avoids lone wolves with big personalities. “The real question everyone has to deal with is: are you willing to lose revenue to keep the culture you want? And the best firms say ‘yes’ if they believe in their culture and the strategy they’re building.”

    “I’d rather have five really good partners who are focused on building the right culture and client delivery model than one all-star who’s a jackass,” he added.

    ]]>     2475854Maria Ward-Brennan Maria Ward-Brennan     New McLaren McL 6GT: Inside the design studio reinventing the British supercar https://www.cityam.com/new-mclaren-mcl-6gt-inside-the-design-studio-reinventing-the-british-supercar/ Wed, 11 Nov 2026 06:00:00 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2476116

    We speak to McLaren design boss Kemal Curic about the new-era McL 6GT, and how he plans to reinvigorate the British supercar company]]>

    Kemal Curic is a man on a mission. His goal: to reinvent McLaren and reclaim its seat at the supercar top table.

    For a car designer, it’s both a dream job and a daunting one. However, the McL 6GT (pictured above) suggests Curic has hit the ground running. The retro concept was the star of Monterey Car Week this summer, prompting McLaren to announce a run of 500 customer cars – due in 2028.

    To learn more about how the McL 6GT took shape, I met with Curic at McLaren’s new design studio in Bicester, Oxfordshire. Here, aided by old-fashioned clay models and new-fangled augmented reality tech, I got a glimpse into the British company’s future.

    The McLaren story so far

    McLaren Automotive has achieved a lot in 16 short years. From a standing start in 2010, the original MP4-12C took the fight straight to Ferrari. Just two years later, it was followed by the epochal hybrid P1, then a succession of lauded ‘Longtail’ (LT) models and the 720S. The latter was arguably the most complete supercar of its era – and proved Woking could see off anything from Maranello or Sant’Agata Bolognese.

    More recently, though, while its Formula 1 team has brought home successive world championships, McLaren Automotive hasn’t been so busy spraying champagne. Yes, the W1 hypercar is a sold-out success (399 units at £2 million each – nice work if you can get it), but the company’s core products are all showing their age. Indeed, production of the 750S has just ended, with both the Artura and GTS likely to be phased out next year.

    McLaren’s fightback starts here, then, spearheaded by a £500 million investment from Abu Dhabi’s CYVN Holdings that will create 1,000 new jobs over the next six years. The flagship McLaren Technology Centre in Surrey will be upgraded, the carbon fibre facility in Sheffield will double in size and a new factory at an as-yet-undisclosed UK location is on the cards, too. A replacement for the 750S – which we know will be called McL 820 – arrives in 2027 and, inevitably, an SUV looms large on the horizon. Defining what makes a McLaren has never been more difficult. Over to you, Kemal…

    Inside McLaren’s new design studio

    From the outside, McLaren’s design office looks like any other new-build industrial unit. However, after I sign in and seal my phone inside a protective pouch – to prevent any ‘scoop’ photos of half-finished prototypes – I can enter the inner sanctum: a calming and spacious studio flooded with natural light. This is where the next generation of McLarens are already taking shape.

    I’m greeted by Chief Design Officer Curic and his Design Director, John Paul Gregory, then ushered into a small cinema to watch the launch film for the McL 6GT. In between the pumping beats and clouds of tyre smoke, it claims the car is simultaneously about ‘celebrating our origins’ and ‘the first expression of a new philosophy’. Like many European car manufacturers at present, it seems McLaren is looking backwards to go forwards.

    You can’t argue with the results, though. After many years of being criticised for cars that looked too similar, the McL 6GT feels like a clean slate: a move away from aero-optimised aggression to something simpler and more classically beautiful. “It answers the question: ‘What would Bruce McLaren drive today?’” says Curic.

    A guiding star for the McL 6GT

    In fact, the McL 6GT reimagines a car that Bruce McLaren did drive. Decades before the McLaren F1 came along, the company founder had plans to create its first road-going supercar. The result was the M6GT (pictured above), a wedge-shaped projectile based on the M6A Can-Am racer. It featured a fibreglass body draped over an aluminium monocoque, butterfly doors and a brawny, mid-mounted Chevrolet V8.

    Although we didn’t realise it at the time, McLaren pre-empted the arrival of the McL 6GT with an in-house M6GT restoration. Based on one of the three original prototypes and lovingly crafted over 3,000 hours by McLaren Special Operations (MSO), it took a bow at Goodwood Festival of Speed in July, a month before the McL 6GT debuted in California.

Other design elements that nod to the past include the tail lights and air vents in the rear window. Their straight-sided oval shape echoes the same motif on the McLaren F1.

    The clay model is impressive – only its opaque ‘windows’ give the game away – but what happens next is still more so: a chance to explore the McL 6GT in augmented reality.

    I strap on a pair of Apple Vision Pro goggles and, like magic, a virtual McLaren appears in front of me. The car is rendered in millimetre-perfect 3D clarity, and the image shifts seamlessly as I walk around it. It’s disorientating at first, particularly when you realise you can pass a hand through the ‘physical’ object, but must be an invaluable way for designers to communicate their ideas – particularly with colleagues in other parts of the world.

    Using a bespoke interior buck fitted with two seats and a steering wheel, I’m then able to climb inside the McL 6GT and enjoy a driver’s eye view. The carbon tub is (deliberately) visible when you swing the doors upwards, while the square quilting on the seats is another element drawn from the 1969 M6GT. The wheel is devoid of any buttons, in trademark McLaren style, with rocker switches either side of the instrument binnacle to adjust the drive modes. A long throttle pedal in anodised ‘Papaya’ aluminium is a bold statement of intent, too.

The exposed linkage looks beautiful, as does the hollowed-out gear knob atop a stubby lever. It might be slower around a circuit than a car with a dual-clutch ’box and paddles, but who cares? “We obsess over tactility, including how the gearshift feels,” says Curic, who seems to be reading my mind. “Ordinarily, you can interact with our cars without ever taking your hands off the steering wheel. The McL 6GT is a bit different.”

    The road ahead for McLaren

    Want one? Of course you do. Yet it’s a safe bet all 500 examples of the McL 6GT have already been sold, even before McLaren has publicly disclosed a price.

    Still, it’s what this car represents, rather than its profit potential, that is most exciting for folk in Woking, Sheffield and Bicester: a fresh design direction, and proof that even its ‘Ultimate Series’ models don’t have to slavishly chase speed and lap times to be achingly desirable.

Yet increasing disillusionment with modern supercars, coupled with the rise of the restomod, suggests that is what many buyers want.

    From universal childcare to R&D funding for start-ups, tech companies must look at smart ways to get communities to buy in to the AI revolution, says Paul Ormerod

    The recent midterm elections in America have already generated a massive amount of media commentary. Most of it of course is on the potential political ramifications.

    But there was an important economic aspect to both the campaigns and the results. Namely, the antipathy which emerged towards AI. This was symbolised in the results of 45 local referendums which took place on data centres. In 44 of these the proposal for a data centre was rejected.

    Democrat candidates were particularly vociferous in their hostility towards both the centres and the technology in general. This is hardly surprising, given the enormous support they attract from liberal arts graduates whose lifestyles and employment are being undermined by AI.

    A coordinated campaign against data centres took place across Europe last weekend. Most were peaceful but in Amsterdam substantial damage was inflicted on a Microsoft data centre construction site.

    An easy characterisation of these events is to label the voters and protesters as Luddites. The original Luddite movement peaked nationally in the decade of the 1810s, protesting against how the revolutionary technology of machines was slashing the wages, often of previously high skilled and high paid (for the time) workers.

    Machinery was smashed, and the British government responded by making it an offence punishable by either transportation or death.

    Despite this, social unrest persisted into the 1840s. But in the end, the Luddites lost and “machinery” prevailed. There was massive economic disruption, and many skilled workers were driven into acute poverty. But the overall benefits were far too substantial to be ignored.

    The same will eventually happen this time round with AI. Apart from anything else, countries like China and India are hardly going to pause development simply because members of the middle class are being made downwardly mobile in the West.

    The next industrial revolution

    But we ought to be able to manage the transition better than we did in the first Industrial Revolution 200 years ago.

    A paper published earlier this year by Daniel Goetz and colleagues at the prestigious Brookings Institute in the US does not offer a complete solution. But it does give some important pointers around data centres themselves.

    The authors acknowledge that a data centre as such does little for the local economy. There are some construction jobs, but few permanent jobs in the centre itself. True, they are well paid, but otherwise a data centre is not that much different to a logistics warehouse. It does not contribute to the transformation of future prosperity in the area.

    A data centre may of course attract more high-tech companies to locate near it. 

    But the Brookings report offers more immediate and productive guidelines. These are based on deals which have either already been done or are in active discussion with local and state authorities in the United States.

    The authors point out, for example, oil and gas rich states have already received direct payments from oil revenues, through state-operated entities like the Alaska Permanent Fund and the North Dakota Legacy Fund. More recently, New Mexico created a $7bn fund for universal childcare, using endowment revenues from the oil and gas industry. Similar principles can be applied to AI developments.

    Local agenda can be developed for enhancing high-tech talent initiatives at local institutions and schools. Alternatively, they might involve securing abundant computing resources for local academic work from an incoming hyper-scaler, or they could entail enlisting partnerships in other forms of R&D at local universities, start-up companies, or entrepreneurial energy companies.

    These are early days. But in America, at least, companies in the AI sector are beginning to engage in meaningful ways with local communities to generate outcomes which benefit everyone.

    Paul Ormerod is an Honorary Professor at the Alliance Business School at the University of Manchester. You can follow hm on Instagram @profpaulormerod
