    Global development progress has stalled as rich nations shift aid budgets toward climate mitigation, but focusing resources on high-return investments in health, education, and economic growth offers the most effective path to uplift the world’s poorest, say Indermit Gill and Bjorn Lomborg

    The last 75 years have brought the greatest improvement of human welfare in history. But over the past decade, much of that progress has stalled. This happened at the same time that the rich world shifted its attention to climate change. This is not a coincidence, and it has to change.

    Consider extreme poverty, long defined as living on less than a dollar a day. In 1950, more than half of humanity was that poor. Today the share is 7.6 per cent, the lowest ever recorded. Average schooling has almost tripled, from 3.2 years to nearly nine. Electricity access has soared. Problems remain, but the gains have been spectacular.

    Now development has slowed to a crawl. After almost two centuries of declining poverty, the number of poor people hasn’t budged since 2016. Global progress is at its slowest pace since 1950, according to the World Bank.

    There are many causes but one stands out. In 2016, the world retired its Millennium Development Goals – a shortlist of mostly efficient, targeted aims: cut poverty, disease, maternal and child deaths and get every child into school. In their place came the Sustainable Development Goals. Climate change became the rich world’s obsession.

    Helping the poorest

    Nowhere is this obsession clearer than in the rich world development aid. Its core purpose is to help development, yet increasingly money is instead spent on climate. In the United Kingdom, climate-tagged finance accounted for 26.7 per cent of its development-aid commitments in 2024, or $4.342bn. Across the rich world, $49bn or nearly a quarter of all development commitments is climate. It is even more pronounced for the global development banks that now spend half its development money on climate, at about $103bn for low- and middle-income countries.

    Both Britain’s Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office and the development banks seem to have convinced themselves that because poor people are more vulnerable to climate change, climate policy is crucial for development. The logic is seductive but wrong. Poor people are more vulnerable to everything – disease, hunger, broken infrastructure and economic shocks. The real question is whether climate policy is the best way to help them. Examined rigorously, development generally wins decisively.

    Sustained economic growth is the surest predictor of a country’s ability to withstand climate shocks. A 10 per cent rise in per capita gross domestic product can cut the number of people most exposed to climate disruption by 100m. Prosperity is the ultimate climate adaptation strategy. A hurricane kills hundreds in poor Haiti; the same storm merely inconveniences wealthy Florida. Resilience runs through development – not through a solar farm that raises power prices and slows industrialization.

    The core problem is opportunity cost. Every dollar subsidizing solar panels or carbon accounting is a dollar not spent on schools, maternal health or clean water. Research by the Copenhagen Consensus, with more than 100 economists and several Nobel laureates, compared the returns. Investments in nutrition, health and education routinely deliver $40 to $110 in social benefits per dollar. Climate-mitigation investments – funding emissions cuts in poor countries – often deliver much less back.

    The trade-offs are concrete. For $2.50, an expectant mother can receive micronutrient supplements that prevent stunting and lifelong cognitive damage in her child – returning nearly $100 of long-term benefits. Expanding diagnosis and treatment for tuberculosis and malaria, which still kill more than a million people a year, returns more than $45 for each dollar invested.

    The energy dimension is starkest. Much of Africa uses less electricity per person than a single refrigerator in a Western home. The rich world built its wealth on cheap, reliable fossil fuels, which still supply over 80 per cent of global energy. Yet most rich world development agencies and most development banks now refuse to finance new fossil-fuel projects in poor countries. Germany has spent over €700bn on its energy transition since 2002; power prices more than doubled and its economy is still almost four-fifths fossil fueled. To demand that African nations achieve what Germany cannot – with a fraction of the resources – isn’t climate leadership. It is hypocrisy.

    None of this requires abandoning climate, with both adaptation and green innovation delivering strong returns.

    But the rich world’s development institutions must overcome their climate fixation. The United Kingdom should learn from Norway’s official analysis: an expert group has recommended the government separate climate financing and other global public goods from the development budget. This would mean the money set aside for the world’s poorest would go to actually help them.

    Most of humanity is still quite poor. To help, the rich world should spend billions on tackling urgent, cheaply solved problems before spending trillions to nudge the thermometer in a century. Tellingly, Africans ranked climate change 31st among 34 priorities in a recent Afrobarometer survey. We must rediscover the smart, focused development solutions that transformed the world in the past 75 years – and put the best development policies first.

    Indermit Gill is former chief economist of the World Bank and Bjorn Lomborg is president of the Copenhagen Consensus

    Should UK shops stay be allowed to open for longer than six hours on Sundays? We hear the case for and against in today’s Debate

    YES: The way we shop has changed drastically since 1994 when these laws were imposed

    The current restrictions on Sunday trading were imposed in 1994 in England and Wales to protect Sunday as a shared day of rest, particularly for retail workers, but since then, the way in which we shop has changed out of all recognition. Sunday has become a day when many families choose to shop together, and with the increase in part-time working, retail workers can more easily choose their days off. There is also the impact of online trading with more than a quarter of sales taking place online and many consumers choosing to carry out research online before making their purchase.  

    In my 30+ years in retail law, I know that nothing beats the in-store experience. We’re seeing high quality, exciting brands planting their flagship stores in London and the pedestrianisation of Oxford Street will hopefully lead the way for other town centres to follow suit. We need to regenerate our town centres outside of London and a relaxation of the rules on Sunday trading can only help achieve this. Plus, we need to cater for those shoppers who choose not to shop online.

    Many senior consumers have never been comfortable with online shopping, and the rise of AI and online scams is starting to impact consumer trust. Over 90 per cent of shoppers are concerned about AI-driven risks, including fake businesses created with AI content (94 per cent), AI-generated phishing emails impersonating retailers (93 per cent) and fake product reviews written by AI (91 per cent), according to the State of Ecommerce Trust’s 2026 research. 

    Relaxing the restrictions on Sunday trading gives the UK the perfect opportunity to regenerate town centres. It gives customers the choice as to when and how they shop and it allows retail businesses to offer that choice.  

    Caroline Green is a partner at law firm Browne Jacobson specialising in retail

    NO: Supporters of extended opening hours are unable to prove the economic benefits

    The Sunday Trading Act is a fair compromise between competing views. The Union of Shop, Distributive and Allied Workers’ (Usdaw) members remain overwhelmingly opposed to extending Sunday trading hours. Allowing large stores to open for longer on Sundays would have a negative impact on retail workers, their families and our communities.

    Longer Sunday trading would take a heavy toll on staff who would come under even more pressure to work, when they would rather be spending time with family and engaging in community, sports and leisure activities or attending church.

    There would also be a detrimental impact on smaller retailers who can already open longer hours on Sundays. These traders rely on the boost in trade they get before and after large stores are allowed to open on Sunday. Even supporters of extended Sunday opening hours have not been able to show it will lead to economic benefits or job creation. Put simply, opening shops for longer does not mean people have more money to spend.

    An experiment with extended Sunday trading during the 2012 Olympic Games was a flop. Usdaw reps reported that in large stores that opened for longer during the Games, over two-thirds were quiet or empty and only five per cent were busy during the extra hours. Many stores reduced their opening times after the first few weeks because they realised that opening for longer didn’t bring more custom, but did increase overheads, and was therefore bad for business.

    There are many more issues that need to be addressed to help retail recover, including a fair business rates system to level the playing field with online, action to tackle high levels of theft from shops and attacks on shop workers, along with supporting councils to invest in high streets.

    Joanne Thomas is general secretary of Usdaw

    THE VERDICT

    Liberalising UK Sunday trading laws – which currently prevent shops larger than 280 square metres from opening for more than six hours on the Lord’s day – is a discussion that’s been revisited ever since the rules were first put in place in 1994, and seems to have been infected with the kind of it’s-just-not-gonna-happen resignation that often plagues exciting projects. 

    Opponents defend the restrictions for a myriad of causes, from faith-related causes to the protection of retail workers’ leisure time, along with an economic argument – perhaps most pertinent to City AM’s readers – that longer Sunday opening hours do not generate sales, just displace them. 

    Recent results from toy shop The Entertainer, however, perhaps offers a counter to the latter. Since opening its toy shops on Sundays – restricted before September 2025 due to the beliefs of its Christian owners – The Entertainer has seen a 10 per cent uptick in sales, which surely presents at least one economic case study for liberalising trading laws. And besides, if opening for longer hours didn’t serve businesses’ bottom lines, those businesses would be at full liberty to still choose to operate by their previous hours.

    Recently, the boss of Selfridges also called for a renewed look at the laws, which currently mean the department shop does not start selling goods until midday on a Sunday, which he feels is limiting the high street’s potential. 

    As pedestrianisation (a project that looks set to prove the potential of big swings) transforms Oxford Street, extending Sunday opening hours could be another needed shot in the arm for British retail. And if it feels like one of those things that just won’t change, we would do well to recall before 1994, when trading on Sundays wasn’t allowed at all.

    Professional services giant Accenture has asked the Court of Appeal to reinstate a ruling that meant it didn’t have to pay a former manager ‘unfairly dismissed’ compensation.

    A former management consultant, Sanju Pal, who worked at the firm for 10 years, was dismissed in July 2019 under Accenture’s ‘up or elsewhere’ progression-based performance model. This framework, standard in professional services firms, means employees must demonstrate that they are progressing toward the next grade level, and failing to stay on a promotion track is treated as underperformance.

    Pal received consecutive ‘not progressing’ performance ratings in August 2018 and March 2019, but during that time, she was diagnosed with endometriosis, which is a chronic medical condition that affects the wombs. This led to periods of sickness absence and a phased return to work.

    She later filed an employment claim against the firm, alleging unfair dismissal and disability discrimination.

    In 2022, the Employment Tribunal (ET) agreed that the dismissal was procedurally unfair because Accenture breached its own disciplinary and appeals policy by using a misconduct route and failing to involve independent decision-makers. However, despite finding the dismissal unfair, the ET applied a 100 per cent reduction (known as polkey), resulting in no compensation for lost earnings.

    The ET also dismissed her discrimination claim, ruling that her endometriosis did not meet the legal definition of a disability under the Equality Act 2010.

    Tribunal errors force new hearing

    The case went to the Employment Appeal Tribunal (EAT), and in January 2026, Judge James Tayler ruled the ET made errors when applying the 100 per cent reduction in compensation. He held that the ET cannot assume an ‘up or out’ policy automatically justifies firing someone who is perfectly capable of fulfilling their current contracted role, so the compensation shouldn’t have been reduced.

    The EAT also found the ET’s dismissal of her disability status was “wholly inadequate” and that the ET failed to properly analyse the medical evidence, the impact on her day-to-day activities, and the likelihood of her endometriosis recurring.

    Judge Tayler allowed Pal’s appeal and directed that the case be remitted to the Employment Tribunal for a fresh hearing before a different panel.

    Following this judgment, Emma Clark, partner and Imogen Dale, associate at Keystone Law, said the ruling “sends a clear message to employers about handling long-term health conditions with care. Employers must look beyond absence statistics and engage meaningfully with reasonable adjustments.”

    Following the EAT judgment, Accenture appealed to the Court of Appeal, seeking to have the second-highest court in the UK restore the original 2022 Tribunal decision.

    The New York-listed firm’s appeal case is before Lord Justice Bean, Lord Justice Baker, and Lady Justice Whipple on Tuesday and Wednesday.

    Accenture said in a statement: “The original Employment Tribunal determined that Sanju Pal’s dismissal was on grounds of performance and was not due to her medical condition, or discriminatory reasons.

    Subsequent legal proceedings have not changed the Tribunal’s decision, though a new hearing will reconsider some of the issues. As legal proceedings are ongoing, we cannot comment further about the details of the case.”

    Number 11’s fixation with tinkering with ISAs is testament to their success, writes James Ashton

Building societies like the flows into Cash ISAs to underwrite the mortgages that account for the other half of their business, while many stock market-listed companies want to see a portion of this giant £420bn cash pile deployed in Stocks and Shares ISAs to bolster their share price.

The industry-backed Invest for the Future campaign – the one that features Savvy the Squirrel – aims to shift long-standing perceptions and support more people in seeing investing as something for them, the natural next step from saving. So-called “targeted support”, launched in April, should make it easier to get that message over.

    However, the reality for many is it is hard to put anything away, not least because the growth in real household disposable income this decade is on course to be the worst on record, the Resolution Foundation projects.

One of its strands intends to make it easier for employers to offer workplace savings schemes, an acknowledgement that salting away a few pounds per month directly from a person’s payslip can be habit forming.     While the UK changes its mind over ISAs, innovation is taking place elsewhere. The tax-free savings amount for Sweden’s well-liked ISK savings product doubled this year and the range of eligible assets is being broadened – although the effective tax rate is rising too.

Such inertia reminds me that the ISA limit last rose in 2017. If £20,000 then had kept track with inflation now, it would be worth more than £27,000 – excellent news for the circa 2m savers who typically max out their ISA annually.

    Of course, many savers can only dream of setting so much aside. But dreams are a good start for getting to grips with individual financial realities, whatever system the Chancellor of the day puts in place.

    We live in a world of radical transparency where nothing is off limits. If you are a successful booming tech company, the geo-political implications are massive. Authoritarians and rogue states are  willing to do anything to get an advantage. Executives (and indeed all employees) in these companies need to be on the lookout. To quote Andy Grove, the former chief executive of Intel, “only the paranoid survive”.

A good friend who used to work for a former PM of  a strong UK ally was warned about honey traps by his country’s security services before heading to a pariah state. “Remember,” they said, “If you are a five out of ten at home, you are a five out of ten on the road.” Salient advice.

    Couple this with the fact there are multiple routes to exposure thanks to tech and social media. Everyone can be a whistle-blower, everyone can be an amateur journalist, airing their grievances on a platform of their choice hoping their clip might go viral. The result in some instances is millions are wiped off share prices and the lifespan of CEOs are radically reduced.

    Corporate governance will now have to cover personal conduct in a way it has, to date, not. Nothing can be hidden. The threat of malign state entities and unscrupulous commercial actors of taking down big tech companies who are in some cases, more powerful than governments, has never been greater. 

    A class act

    The steady growth of class actions in the UK has put the behaviour of big companies in the spotlight. One bubbling away in the background that deserves a lot more press scrutiny involves the high street brand Johnson and Johnson.

    Several thousand claimants represented by KP Law have accused the company of selling talcum powder contained with contaminants linked to cancer. J&J for their part vehemently deny the claims saying the product was compliant with regulatory standards.

    The claim is set to become the largest product liability case in UK history.

    The trial is listed for 2028 so a verdict is a way off. However the growth in the wider class action regime is a positive move giving access to justice for thousands who previously had no legal recourse.

    Quote of the week

    “These increases should not be seen as the first of an inevitable long sequence of hikes. That is not inevitable.”

    Andrew Bailey on another potential interest rate hike

    Dubai doesn’t deserve all the flak

    I have been in Dubai this week. It has come in for a lot of flak recently but compare it to a crime-ridden London where police estimates suggest more than 70,000 mobile phones are swiped every year. Probably only in Dubai (and maybe Singapore) can you safely leave your mobile phone on a table in a bar for hours on end. The same goes for your personal safety – men and women can walk around at four in the morning without any fear of being mugged. London could learn a lot from the UAE.

    London is a culinary capital

    London has transformed itself into a culinary destination over the past two decades so it was to my surprise to learn that the capital only has two Michelin star-rated pubs. The Kerfield Arms in Camberwell is one. It got the award in February this year, less than 12 months after opening. The food is exquisite and the wine list rivals any top London restaurant. Let’s hope the 20 per cent cut in business rates for them coming into force next year gives them a much-needed boost.

    The world of watches is often buried beneath glossy PR scripts, corporate data sheets, and carefully rehearsed press events. Making Time is a chance to strip all that away by pulling up a chair with some of the industry’s most influential figures and passionate watch collectors, a chance to talk about the human reality of collecting: the emotional side of the pursuit, the regrets, the hard choices and, above all, the passion.

    Andy Blackmore: So, what’s on your wrist today, and why?

    AB: How many watches do you own? Do you know off the top of your head or would you have to check?

    TDH: I’m not a big watch collector – I think I have 10 or 11. Certainly not all A Lange watches. I have a Lange watch, Seikos, two Longines and an IWC from the early days when I worked there.

    AB: What takes you longer: deciding on your shoes or your watch?

    TDH: Shoes. Because for shoes I have to think, ‘Okay, what kind of suit or jeans or trousers do I put on?’ That takes more time, because I need to look at other stuff to combine. A watch is just like, boom! I am in an excellent position that I can’t go wrong with the watch I wear, of course.

    His first watch: A Longines automatic

    AB: What was the first proper watch you bought with your own money?

    TDH: It was a Longines automatic. L919 calibre. It was a used watch from 1979, a double barrel, very nice, thin movement. I still have it.

    AB: And I’ve still got my grandfather’s solid gold Longines. Is there a style of watch you actively avoid? Anything too flashy, dressy or trendy?

    TDH: Yeah, I’m not a trendy guy. I’m more about timeless – I’ve been too long at A Lange & Söhne! I like the timelessness of the design. I’m not a fan of, ‘Oh wow, that’s cool! A watch with a green dial,’ or something like that. I think timelessness and quality is more important. Or emotion, you know? Memories. When I was 10, I got a Seiko 5 from my parents, an automatic, and I still have it. That’s an emotional thing.

    AB: I know you said you’re not much of a watch collector, but would picking up a genuine classic for a song on eBay or in a flea market still give you a buzz?

    TDH: No.

    AB: Do you wear every watch you own, or are some too precious?

    TDH: No, I wear everything I have.

    AB: If the house is on fire, what single watch would you grab?

    TDH: My Lange! That’s the only one. Or maybe the first Seiko from my parents.

    AB: Is that your most precious watch?

    TDH: Emotionally, yes.

    The Longines that found its way back

    AB: Is there a watch in your collection that has a personal story that’s got nothing to do with watchmaking?

    TDH: I have one. I did watchmaking school in Holland, for four years. The first three years you do school, and then you do your exam, and then you have your internship in the last year. I went and worked at a watch shop with two watchmakers and three goldsmiths.

    The owner said, ‘You know what? That’s a nice project for you. You restore that watch, and then we sell it. Learn how to polish the case, redo everything, order the parts…’ So I restored the watch, and I really loved it. When I finished it, he said I’d done an excellent job and he put it in the shop window. I wanted to buy it but I couldn’t afford it. Two days later, he said, ‘Congratulations, I sold the watch’.

    AB: Is there a watch you regret buying?

    TDH: Hm. Not really. I’m a big fan of the IWC Porsche Design watches from the 80s and 90s, the titanium ones.     TDH: I met someone wearing a special edition of the Ocean 2000 Porsche Design IWC diver, one that was made for the German navy. They had a black bezel and a red hand. I used to repair them! I stopped them to say ‘That’s a very special watch’.

    AB: Do you ever worry you take watches too seriously?

    Father-daughter duo Chris and Emily Boxall are using microlearning and gamification to tackle the UK's financial knowledge crisis via their app, 2mins]]>

    The UK has one of the lowest levels of financial literacy in the developed world. A 2024 Santander study found that only 47 per cent of UK adults could correctly answer at least five out of seven financial knowledge questions, compared with 62 per cent across OECD countries. The same survey found that only 1 per cent of primary school teachers believed their pupils had adequate financial skills.

    The government is expanding financial literacy through curriculum mandates and the HM Treasury’s Financial Inclusion Strategy, under which financial education will become statutory in primary schools across England starting in Autumn 2028. But critics argue this will still leave millions of children each year woefully unprepared for real life.

    That challenge inspired Emily Boxall and her father, Chris, to set up their edTech startup 2mins to try and address this growing problem.

    The genesis of the idea came from Chris’s interactions with clients at Fundamental Asset Management, many of whom were wealthy, sophisticated investors who simply valued plain-English clarity over industry jargon. “I think it was at this point that I realised that I could bring something”, says Emily. “I felt like I could bring the solution because I’ve got this different way of thinking about things,” she adds.

    The team ended up creating 2mins, an app designed to teach users about money through a series of original, engaging, and challenging games. Since launching in January, 2mins has attracted over 2,000 users, who compete against each other to rack up the highest scores by playing a series of games every week. Games are designed, as the name suggests, to be played in 2mins, a name and format chosen to remove some of the stigma associated with financial education. Emily has taken on the role of chief games creator, developing the idea of each game and then putting that idea into practice with the help of AI.

    Initially, Emily says they received critical feedback about the nature of the games and, in particular, the animals. “I asked if we needed to change it to fit all the feedback?” Emily explained. “But we said no; we’re doing this to be different, to be bold, and we’re trying to reach people who haven’t been reached before by this. And we stuck with it. And I’m so glad that we have.”

    2mins: A tool for schools

    Now being piloted in nine schools across the UK, 2mins aims to make financial education easier for teachers to deliver and more engaging for students. While the government has taken important steps to put financial education on the curriculum, there’s still a lot to do. And telling schools to do something doesn’t necessarily mean they will.

    Schools and teachers are constrained by time and resources. That’s where Emily and Chris believe they have an edge. “When schools need to deliver financial education as part of the curriculum, hopefully they’ll look to 2mins as a really accessible, easy way to deliver that education”, Emily explains.

    While schools are a key focus of its current expansion, 2mins was originally designed for users aged 16 and over and has also attracted an enthusiastic adult following. “We’ve got a lovely group of over 45-year-old women playing,” says Emily, highlighting one example. The next version of the app will also be designed with teachers in mind, following lessons learned during the testing phase.

    “It is about trying to engage the teacher; I think that’s the hardest part; it’s less about the student, more about the teacher,” Chris explains. “That’s probably the hardest thing that was a bit of an unknown,” he adds.

    The corporate market

    The father-daughter team are also developing the app for a rather different market: corporate HR departments.

    The business is currently in discussions with a major corporate client to develop an app for new starters and younger employees, helping them navigate incentives and benefits on offer, from pension entitlement to share schemes and even parental leave.

    The corporate version will build on the same principles as the original app, with bespoke content and branding designed around each company’s employee benefits, culture and objectives. The aim is to create something that’s “fun and light-hearted” that the company’s employees still want to engage with. “The last thing users want is to be lectured or educated in the formal sense,” Chris says.

    Creating products for this market, Chris says, was always a long-term goal once 2mins proved itself with the most demanding audience: young people.

    Following the completion of its initial schools pilot, Emily and Chris plan to roll out an enhanced version of 2mins in 2027, initially targeting independent schools with a paid subscription model and a dedicated teacher dashboard. At the same time, they want to continue developing the corporate product to cultivate this potentially lucrative market and attract a sponsor to help fund the rollout across state schools.

    By combining gamification with accessible microlearning, 2mins is working to transform financial literacy for pupils and employees alike. Its success was recognised earlier this year when 2mins was awarded the runner-up award at The Money Awareness and Inclusion Awards for Best Fintech/AI by a For Profit Organisation, and the winner of Best Content Creation at the Financial Capability Awards.

    As the app moves toward nationwide expansion, Emily and Chris Boxall’s innovative approach offers a promising solution to bridge the UK’s financial knowledge gap and empower the next generation.

    Around $2bn was staked on prediction markets across last week’s US midterm elections, yet sites like Polymarket and Kalshi aren’t categorised as bookmakers across the pond.

    The sector is rapidly growing, with binary markets becoming subject to increased spend across America: how many tweets Elon Musk will post on X today is a real market, alongside the next Democratic presidential nominee, the price of Bitcoin at 6am tomorrow morning and what Anthropic’s IPO closing market cap will be.

    It has led to a number of contracts across American sport, with a deal between Major League Baseball and Polymarket potentially worth over £200m. The NBA last month got on the bandwagon, announcing partnerships with both Kalshi and Polymarket. So are they coming to the Premier League, Hundred or other UK competitions? 

    The reality is that prediction markets would need to penetrate a very mature betting market to operate in the UK. From a scratchcard at 16 to a bingo hall at 86 – and everything in between – the British betting market is already varied and very closely regulated. The closest thing the UK has to a prediction market lever – betting exchanges like Betfair – are monitored by the Gambling Commission.

    Combined with oversight from the Financial Conduct Authority and the costs associated with obtaining a licence to operate here, it is more likely that prediction markets would follow the playbook of Asian betting sites, which are inaccessible to Brits but have spent big on UK sponsorships with global reach, such as Premier League football clubs.

    Regulation on the way?

    “Regulation is the significant barrier for entry, rather than any demand concern,” sport finance expert Professor Rob Wilson tells City AM. “The US markets see them positioned as a type of financial exchange whereas the UK indicates they’re more like gambling operators hence the licensing requirement.

    “These are well capitalised, ambitious businesses competing for visibility and market share. Sport offers exactly what they need, especially where there are global audiences and quick brand recognition. We’ve already seen crypto play in this area, so I sense these are next.”

    One major problem that could affect prediction markets in sport sponsorship, however, is the government’s consultation on banning unlicensed gambling brands. While prediction markets do not see themselves as casino products in the US, that description may not fly so well in the UK.

    Regulatory hoops might mean that sponsorship is the only way in, by any means necessary, perhaps as a partner of US-facing properties like the NBA game in Manchester next January, or when the NFL comes to London. The deal between Polymarket and the UFC could find itself into the O2 arena sooner rather than later. 

    Prediction markets realities

    “In terms of what kind of deal we could see,” Wilson adds, “It will probably be official prediction market partnerships through the usual digital inventory and activation.

    “It’ll involve broadcast integration and data sweating to deliver fan engagement. The platforms are built around engagement and sport, quite naturally, provides a continuous stream of events to trade on.

    “We know overseas sponsorship strategy already happens and the reach is significant so there’s no reason why they wouldn’t pursue a similar strategy. The issue will be the UK government regulating out betting sponsorship.”

    Added a Betting and Gaming Council spokesperson: “Betting and gaming operators in the UK are subject to strict regulation by the Gambling Commission, and any prediction-style market operators would need to be licensed and meet those same robust standards.”

    It is a sector that feels both distant and very present, but prediction markets are coming in some way, shape or form. The UK appears to be on top of the regulation but, like crypto, the cash potential is high and whether sport can ignore it creeping onto these shores will be a question for the coming seasons.

    London's centuries-old cigar trade and thriving lounge scene make it the world's best city for hand-rolled cigar smokers, says The Emory's head of cigars, Blue Curran.]]>

    London is, without a doubt, the best city in the world for hand-rolled cigar smokers, explains Blue Curran, head of cigars at The Emory Cigar Merchants.

    The city’s edge lies in its history. Smokers have bought, sold, imported and exported cigars from London for centuries, and that means the capital has one of the biggest reserves of cigars anywhere in the world.

    London’s cigar debut occurred in 1814, when British officers returned from the Peninsular War carrying gifts from their Spanish comrades. The product was snapped up by Britain’s smokers in the thousands of tobacco houses, private clubs and pubs across the country. The first cigar manufacturer in London was William Kelly and Sons, which opened in 1870, and over the following years the industry continued to put down roots in the capital.

    In the 20th Century, names such as Alfred Dunhill and Davidoff of London opened their doors, joining Robert Lewis, founded in 1787 on St James’s Street, which later counted Sir Winston Churchill and Oscar Wilde among its customers. In 1992, it joined forces with James J. Fox. Sautter of Mount Street also joined the collection.

    Most of these names still have a presence in the city despite policymakers’ attempts to clamp down on smoking. There’s also a thriving cigar lounge scene, with locations such as The Emory Cigar Merchants, The Connaught Cigar Merchants and the Garden Room at the Lanesborough Hotel on Hyde Park Corner.

    Although smoking indoors is generally illegal in the UK, the law permits dedicated, specialist cigar shops to have an indoor tasting or sampling room where customers can smoke cigars or pipe tobacco. That’s why rooms like those found in The Emory are technically classed as cigar shops.

    The life of a hand-rolled cigar

    Outsiders and non-smokers often lump cigarettes and cigars into the same category, but as Blue explains, they could not be more different.

    Hand-rolled cigars make up four per cent of the global cigar market by volume, but nearly a third of the overall market value. Machine-manufactured cigars make up the remainder. Unlike the mass-produced machine-made cigars, it can take years to learn the art of cigar rolling, and many days to roll an individual cigar.

    Cuba is the spiritual home of the cigar, but due to export restrictions and output limitations, the market today is dominated by other Central American countries such as Ecuador and Nicaragua, as well as the Dominican Republic.

    The most common hand-rolled cigar size is the so-called Robusto size. A short, thick cigar that measures roughly 5 inches in length with a 50 ring gauge (typically ranging from 4.75 to 5.5 inches long and 48 to 52 ring gauge). These can take five years to grow and roll with care, going through every stage of the growing and production process. Each cigar contains at least four different tobacco leaves: a binder leaf to hold it all together and a wrapper leaf on top.

    These are vital to the cigar’s taste and curated for the perfect look and feel and are the largest type of leaf you’ll find in a cigar. Selected for size, colour and a lack of imperfections, these leaves are often grown under canopies, such as cheesecloth, that diffuse direct sunlight and alter how the plant grows. This ultimately makes the leaves stretchier, smoother and thinner.

    Ultimately, each cigar has a unique taste and flavour. When stored properly in a controlled environment (typically around 65 per cent to 70 per cent relative humidity and 18°C to 21°C), cigars can last for decades, or even a century. Older cigars lose some of their harshness, replaced by sweetness or peppiness, but strength isn’t consistent from brand to brand.

    While the Robusto is the most common, other sizes, such as the Churchill (7 inches long with a ring gauge of 47) are perhaps more associated with the category. The Churchill, named after Sir Winston, an avid cigar smoker, was previously known as a Large Corona, the larger version of the Corona, the benchmark size (5 1/2 to 6 inches) against which all other cigars are measured. Longer, fatter cigars burn at a lower temperature and last much longer than shorter, thinner cigars.

    Cigar smoking in London: how to enjoy it

    “It’s the time and effort that’s gone into the cigar” that makes smoking each one such a special experience, explains Blue. They are not designed to be smoked in a hurry. Cigars are designed to be enjoyed and smoked with friends. They’re meant to pass the time in a friendly way, he adds. “Smoke it how you want,” Blue explains. As long as you are enjoying the experience, don’t let anyone tell you any different.

    “One of the big things about cigar smoking is not coming away smelling of cigars,” explains Blue. That’s a mark of a good cigar lounge, he adds – you should be able to leave after enjoying your time and not carry the smell around.

    Each one of London’s cigar bars and lounges has created its own collection of cigars. These are usually curated by the venue or its dedicated head of cigars, and each collector leaves their unique stamp on the collection. As Blue explains, some collectors prefer older, more unique cigars, which they spend their time scouring the market for. Others may take a more relaxed approach to curation.

    Another reason London has carved out a unique place for cigar smokers and collectors.

    In 1961, the French Alps were in crisis: the traditional industries of agriculture and mining were shrinking and villages were depopulating as the young moved to find work in the cities. Dr Pierre Borrione, a former French Resistance fighter and the mayor of Aime, took a gamble, building two drag lifts in his town. Not only did he manage to reverse the Tarentaise Valley’s decline, but he set in motion the creation of what has become one of the largest and most popular ski areas in the world: Paradiski.

    VIP Ski is marking this 65th anniversary season in style, opening Graciosa, a brand new ski-in, ski-out chalet development in La Plagne, Paradiski’s biggest resort. Set at a snow-sure 2,003m on the Mont St Sauveur piste, Stephanie Adams was among the first guests to check-in.

    What to do in La Plagne

    There are 225 km of runs at La Plagne, with another 200 km in connected resorts within the Paradiski area. 70% of these are at altitudes above 2,000 m so the powder is pretty much guaranteed.

    To feel the wind on your face and get an adrenaline kick before you even click into your skis, take the Aérolive from Roche de Mio to Live 3,000. This is a gondola with two open-air cabins, L’Acrobate and La Funambule (meaning “tightrope walker”). Brace yourself if you are afraid of heights, as it’s more than a little daunting, but with no windows or walls to the cabins, you can lean out and experience a sensation that’s probably the closest you will ever get to flying. Aérolive departs every 15 minutes, as long as the weather is fair, and, reassuringly, passengers are clipped into a safety harness so you definitely won’t fall out!

    One of the most scenic blue runs in La Plagne is accessible from the Plagne Bellecôte sector. It runs alongside the new Riders Nation snow park, where you can detour to try the four freestyle courses, and then down through forest to the villages of Montchavin and Les Coches. There are impressive views of Mont Blanc on the way.

    Apres ski: La Folie Douce

    Did you even visit Paradiski if you didn’t party at La Folie Douce? The Alps’ most famous apres ski venue is a Les Arcs institution, offering a festival-like atmosphere all winter long. New for this season is L’Atelier, a huge events space which changes purpose as the day goes on. Mornings are dedicated to sports, including indoor cycling; there are creative programmes for children in the afternoons; and in the evenings, the decks are open for amateur DJs to show the crowds what they’re made of.

    L’Atelier’s offering complements La Folie Douce’s core events calendar, Unlimited Folie, which platforms the biggest DJs from Paris and Berlin, from international clubs to underground scenes. Dance until dawn – the shots will keep you warm – then grab an hour or two of sleep before catching the first lift of the day.

    The world’s highest comedy festival

    The Paradiski ski season runs until the end of April, so there’s still plenty of time to make an Easter booking. If you’re looking for a last-minute escape, plan your trip to coincide with Paradiski Comedy Club – the world’s highest stand-up comedy festival – from 16-27 February. Held in collaboration with Paris’ Metro Comedy Club, performers use the Vanoise Express cable car as their stage, delivering stand-up routines in English and French as you dangle 380m above the ground.

    Where to stay in La Plagne: Graciosa

    Get your gang together and book VIP Ski’s CLUB Sagarmatha Penthouse, which crowns the Graciosa and sleeps up to 15 guests. The chalet’s panoramic views stretch as far as Mont Blanc, and you can admire the snow-capped mountains and, later, the star-studded night sky from the private hot tub and sauna on the 6th floor terrace. The chef and chalet hosts will ensure your every need is taken care of, all you have to do is relax. Families can make use of Graciosa’s “Bear Cub” and nanny service, so you can be confident the kids are safe and well entertained as you take to the slopes and enjoy the subsequent apres ski.

    Need to know

    In February 2027, fully-catered accommodation at VIP Ski’s CLUB Sagarmatha Penthouse starts from £1,405 per person per week based on two sharing, including scheduled coach transfers from Geneva Airport. Book directly with VIP Ski (vip-chalets.com). A six-day adult ski pass for Paradiski costs £349 (en.la-plagne.com). For ski hire and ski school, visit Oxygene (oxygene.ski).

    There’s a snobbishness that persists about Val Thorens. There’s the view that it’s “soulless” because it’s a comparatively new resort, having opened in 1971. But actually that was so long ago now that the first people born here are facing retirement.

    One of these people is Aurélie Rey, the daughter of one of the founders of the resort, who runs the Alpen Art restaurant in the centre of town. Look Rey in the eyes and tell her that her food is “soulless” and you’ll see what a ridiculous notion this is.

    Also not soulless: Val Thorens’ main square Place Caron, where skiers heading to the slopes converge. I become obsessed with watching the goings on here over morning coffee from my prime position on my slopeside balcony at Hôtel Le Fitz Roy. It’s not breaking news to suggest town squares are good for people watching, although Place Caron is particularly vibey, even for ski resorts.

    Two scenes converge in Val Thorens, at Europe’s highest ski resort. There are those with money who like the fancy but not ridiculously fancy collection of four and five-star hotels, and the young party types who come for the frankly overwhelming opportunity to ski in any direction you like, the music festivals and the nightlife.

    Actually, there’s another set too. The vibe is so potent here that lots of people appear to have no interest in skiing at all. And not in the Courchevel ‘I’m spending a day shopping at Gucci’ way, more that this is just a functioning, authentic, lively town, that just so happens to be ear-bleedingly high.

    The type of person who goes to Val Thorens is my type of human: into the finer things but not a dick about it. I watch every walk of life collide at Place Caron. An octogenarian couple from Monaco turning redder and redder as they squint below the sun at the gulf of mountains; a group of British lads bringing the tone down; and punctual Scandinavians frustrated by all the hubbub. They just want to ski past and get on (in their colourful ski suits they look like the fragmented colour flashes of a hologram). Unless you’re a thorough misery, or Parisian, this hodge-podge of French, Brits, Dutch, Scandinavians and, more recently, Americans means you don’t have to look far for conversation.

    Why Val Thorens is the world’s best ski resort

    How else should I talk about how great Val Thorens is? How about the kilometres of slopes that suit every type of skier, the near-guaranteed snow (we’re at a squiffy 2,300 metres), and direct connection to Les 3 Vallées, the largest ski area in the world, accessible via one pass?

    Val Thorens has won world’s best ski resort for the tenth year out of thirteen at the World Ski Awards, voted for by the public and ski tourism professionals. That accolade drew me in the first place, helping me decide from dozens of similar-sounding places in the Alps that can feel hard to distinguish between.

    Where to stay in Val Thorens: Hôtel Le Fitz Roy

    Hôtel Le Fitz Roy is exactly the Val Thorens ticket: fancy but not stifling, it is a handsome slopeside property with all of the functional necessities, such as ski-in ski-out access, good local food, a nice spa, and a terrace on Place Caron, on which I spent more time than I’d like to admit surveying the action (yes, I skied a bit, but who wants those boots on for more than four hours a day?).

    Vintage resort photos adorn the walls of the common areas, which are lovely and cozy and draw you in for late-afternoon board games, although I often ended up in the underground spa. Rooms are spacious and many have slopeside views, although the ones with the views up the mountain are fine too.

    A highlight is meat straight from the al fresco winter barbecue, cooked by a man who makes it look perfectly ordinary to be barbecuing outdoors in sub-zero temperatures (it was boiling sunshine for most of our trip, which is common given the resort is often above the cloud line).

    We ascend nearly another thousand metres by cable car for our second most memorable meal, though no one is suffering in silence this time. The mountaintop Caron 3200 restaurant, opened just over a year ago, is the highest restaurant in Les 3 Vallées, with spectacular views that feel as if from a plane’s window. We peer down at the clouds and the spread of mountains into Italy and France from the wine bar. There, we have lunch, in the form of an enormous meat and cheese board. We prefer this to the restaurant which, although nice, is fuller – we had the wine bar to ourselves. Order the rest of the bottle and sack off the afternoon’s ski plans to gawp out at this for a few hours. I’d imagine the equally fancy Ice Q, formerly the highest restaurant in Austria and used in the James Bond film Spectre, is fuming.

    Val Thorens nightlife: Pints, fondue and cover bands

    In search of anything that might be called soulless, that night we shake off our boots and wander into town, past local markets and the O’Connell’s Irish pub and The Frog & Roastbeef rock bar where we lived up to the Brits abroad cliche by sinking altogether too many pints.

    Here, Americans – there are a lot of them, as skiing prices Stateside rocket – seem to be enjoying the British cover bands playing Oasis and Blur tracks more than the rest of us, who can bear this type of place for an hour but are drawn to the exit by the inevitable opening chords for Wonderwall. Opposite more obviously touristic restaurants, including a themed Latin American restaurant called Favela, is La Chaumière, a quietly brilliant French restaurant with polished wooden walls and bench seating, where we enjoyed fondue.

    In fact, Val Thorens is chocca with homely places to linger over; for a week there is equal amount of authenticity and heart here as in the more historical Alpine destinations.

    Le Rooftop is another, where waitstaff are just the warmest and the food is generous: duck, great cuts of meat and more fondue. If you want to amp it up, swerve the more clublike apres ski and go for the ostentatious but not overly so La Maison, another of the resort’s oldest restaurants, with its iconic redback chairs and prime slopeside view, where the cocktails are good.

    La Folie Douce: The Alps’ most famous party

    If you want more of the boots-on-table British image of a French ski holiday, La Folie Douce on the Plein Sud run – a blue run, suitable for most skiers – is one of the Alps’ most lauded party spots. La Fruitière is the chic restaurant here: book lunch and pre-game ahead of a dance on the main bar floor, which becomes truly ridiculous by mid-afternoon. Expect champagne pourings, live singers (who stand out half naked in any weather, including blizzards), live saxophonists, dancers, and hundreds of wasted people dancing to electronic music on the tabletops.

    For plenty more options, the main snow front of Rond Point des Pistes has more of this type of nonsense, plus sophisticated restaurants, and runs pretty much the length of the town.

    Is Val Thorens worth it?

    Other places do other things better: sports professionals love Val d’Isere for its no-nonsense ski focus; Meribel, with its treelines and stone-built 1900s restaurants, brings the proper history. But forget box-ticking and go for an all-round vibe at Val Thorens.

    Why do we get our knickers in such a twist for truffles – and the white truffle above all? The Greeks and Romans loved them; the Egyptians ate them dipped in goose fat and the Catholic church described them as sinful.

    Why do they cost so much?

    Given these little fungi’s stubborn inability to be farmed or mass produced, there is a limited supply, which, given their short shelf life, drives prices sky high. They are aphrodisiacs, not just because you’re flashing the cash to potential partners but also because – so the story goes – their musky scent triggers subconscious feelings of attraction and comfort in some humans (and curiously, most female pigs).

    When is white truffle season?

    The black truffle is present in different forms across the year but right now we have hit white truffle season, which runs until December and means we get to eat one of the most expensive ingredients to be found.

    As my invitation to the Alba white truffle fair in Italy’s Piedmont got lost in the post, I did the next best thing and went for lunch at Bocconcino Mayfair.

    The best wine for white truffle: Nebbiolo

    You’ll have spent a hefty amount on this little lump of gold so it would be remiss to order anything that might reduce its pleasure. The best wine for white truffle is a Nebbiolo, a grape that comes from the same region, Piedmont. It’s a pale, ethereal red, tricking the unknowing drinker into thinking it is light in the mouth, but it has taut, fine-boned tannins and layers of dusky flavours from cherry to violets and, almost always, this mushroomy, truffly note. Barolo and Barbaresco are the premium versions, named respectively the “King” and “Queen” of wines. Barolo is aged longer and is structured, powerful and dense with flavour, whereas Barbaresco comes generally from lower slopes and is typically softer. Both are superb and premium.

    If you are looking to snaffle a bargain, then hunt out a Langhe Nebbiolo, which delivers absolute beauty in the glass but at a much more approachable price.

    Eating white truffle at Bocconcino Mayfair

    I drank through a bottle of Langhe Nebbiolo at Bocconcino and it was a joy with their thin, flavourful slivers of beef carpaccio topped with shavings of creamy white truffle, followed by an excellent white risotto, similarly decked out. The table became engulfed in a cloud of truffle perfume. Given their fragility, speed and skill are required and the truffles I was eating at lunch were harvested in Italy only the morning before. So, order the Nebbiolo (or if you prefer a white, then an elegantly oaked chardonnay) and indulge in this brief window of opportunity for one of nature’s greatest delicacies.

    As autumn draws in and the capital gets darker, the season of comfort food takes hold at London restaurants: glorious pies, a melting ribeye or a bubbling lasagne summon you. It’s the type of food that tests your patience as you salivate, waiting to take a first bite, knowingly in danger of burning your mouth if you jump in too soon. These are meals that demand a great red wine to accompany them…

    Liverpool Street Chop House & Tavern: Award-winning pies and steaks

    At The Evolv Collection, we were delighted that our Chop House & Tavern on New Street won the top accolade, Best Restaurant, in City AM’s Toast the City Awards. Deservedly so: Chop House is a venue, where every detail has an authentic place of origin, whether it’s the design (Brand historian Ron Cregan was drafted in from Mulberry and Maybourne hotel group to re-imagine the Conran classic) or the food menu, which has been a lifelong passion-project for chef Mike Reid (last seen on James Martin’s Saturday Kitchen, cooking a sticky toffee beef short rib). Thank you to all the readers who voted in appreciation.

    When dining in Chop House, you will find dramatic trolleys boasting regeneratively farmed, best of British beef alongside the finest pork, lamb and chops in the world. Specialist knives, forged in Peckham, are presented for your choosing. The wine list is beyond extensive. Few London restaurants offer such comfort and theatre this autumn, underpinned by quality and true hospitality.

    I recently dined there with England world cup winning legends Simon Shaw and Andy Gomarsall, watching as they worked their way through the largest T-bone I’ve seen in 20 years serving steaks. Despite the appeal of the meat offering, my preference was for the pies: mutton shoulder shepherd’s, oxtail and beef, beef shin and oyster, roast chicken and pancetta… They are a masterclass in pastry. If served with a magnum of Joseph Drouhin 2022 Gevrey-Chambertin (£380) or a barrel of Barbaresco Bordnin (£305), the cancellation of late afternoon appointments is inevitable. This is what long lunches in the City are all about.

    Cloth Cornhill: A new City favourite in a historic tavern

    When I was in charge at Gaucho and M, I used to saunter from M Threadneedle Street over to Gaucho Gracechurch Street on a daily basis. My favourite route was through the medieval St Michael’s Alley, past the Jamaica Wine House and Ball Court, which is now home to Cloth Cornhill. Formerly known as Simpsons Tavern since 1757, it was saved in part by a public crowdfund campaign led by City AM. This wonderfully atmospheric hideaway is not to be confused with Jeremy King’s offering on the Strand, although the original signage remains.

    Cloth has a small kitchen and thus a sensibly modest menu boasting comforting elements of both St John’s and Liverpool Street Chop House & Tavern. We began with an austere sausage and mustard, purposefully plain, served like prison food (or so I am told). Scallop sashimi missed the spot, drowned in an almond custard of sorts. But things got much better from here: an excellent plate of pickles and cured trout with horseradish. And the star of the snacks and starters: devils on horseback, which I will return for time and time again.

    The venison pie at Cloth has already become the talk of the town. My steak was also sublime, head and shoulders above the City’s steak chains. A smoked pork chop was almost as outstanding as the devils on horseback, and all was devoured with a Domaine de Bellene Nuits-Saint-Georges (£160).

    This is destined to become a new City favourite and one of the best London restaurants to visit this autumn: a similar draw as Soho’s The Devonshire, but with double the substance. The trio of Shoreditch entrepreneurs Sam, Joe and Ben deserve our patronage and our stomachs certainly deserve their food.

    Rosina: The neighbourhood London restaurant worth the booking battle

    And so to SW12, where another admirable entrepreneur, chef Adam Byatt, has opened a new high profile neighbourhood restaurant named Rosina on the former Pomino and Brinkley’s site.

    I have been a fan of Adam (a Phil Howard protege) and his venues since he opened Thyme in a shitty bit of Clapham in 2001. It won critical acclaim but didn’t work out. His greatest success, one Michelin starred Trinity, has been a favourite of my wife and me for some 20 years.

    So it is a delight that Byatt’s Rosina has joined the outstanding (and Michelin recognised) Chez Bruce on Bellevue Road to add value to the lives of those living in the Nightingale Triangle.

    I have visited a few times since opening. The bar has a great buzz, the wine list is superb and the bar food is even better (go straight to the crispy and gooey fried taleggio). Despite being ridiculously difficult to book a table, Rosina is as fine a London neighbourhood restaurant as could aspire to be. Pure hospitality is on display here and the management is first class (which is rare more than a mile out of Mayfair).

    What to order at Rosina

    I began with the tuna crudo, which is as good as you will find at any Japanese omakase counter. The vitello tonnato was also a standout dish, rich with shallots and capers. We loved the fava bean dip and decided to go ‘full Hannibal’ and enjoy it with a fine Chianti (Isole e Olena 2023, about £85. Alternatively there’s a very approachable Barolo Moscino from superstar winemaker Ciara Boschis for £198). For secondi, the ’nduja strozzapreti, lasagne or ‘pasta splendido’ are all excellent options. For mains, the beef cheek or turbot are both standout dishes. All in all, it was an exceptional experience – unless your dining partner ‘Posh’ Henry Hobhouse accompanies you and inhales all of the sharing plates…

    Book these London restaurants early this autumn

    All three London restaurants are certain hits for autumn entertaining and beyond. Book in advance or roll up early doors to avoid disappointment during these darker days.

    He later collaborated with European media outlets including Der Spiegel to publish further materials, including those that sparked investigations by Uefa and the Premier League into Manchester City’s sponsorship agreements and contracts.

    Conservative members are voting on who they want to represent the party at the London mayor elections in 2028. Maurício Alencar spoke to Sara Gezdari, who is hoping to beat Sir James Cleverly and Festus Akinbusoye to the nomination.

    Sara Gezdari says she wants to give back to Britain what it gave to her following a childhood of “constant fear” in Albania. And as a committed Tory, she hopes to offer to the Conservative Party what Margaret Thatcher stood for. 

    After losing as a candidate in the 2024 General Election for the Liberal Democrat-stronghold of Richmond Park, she now hopes to pip Sir James Cleverly and Festus Akinbusoye to the nomination for the Conservatives’ candidate for the London mayor elections in 2028. 

    Thatcher is an unlikely candidate to inspire a London mayoral bid. Britain’s first female prime minister abolished the capital’s former regional administrative body, the Greater London Council, in the 1980s following a fierce feud with its left-wing leader Ken Livingstone – only for it to reappear, and Livingstone as leader, in a new guise under New Labour in the nineties.

    But Gezdari makes clear her motivation. Growing up in communist Albania through the late 1980s, she queued up with her family for bread and milk rations. She was accompanied by a guard in the streets to stop her from being kidnapped and sold for prostitution or organ trafficking. To her, it is clear that her childhood experiences were shaped by socialism – “this mediocrity ideology where you barely survive”. 

    After fleeing to Italy in her teenage years, Gezdari went on to study politics at university. It became clear to her that Thatcher championed all the values that she held. The trailblazing leader was “somebody who would speak about free markets, free enterprise, the rule of law, a woman being a prime minister”. 

    “That’s the reason why I came to London,” Gezdari said in an interview with City AM. 

    “I’d always had people asking me questions like ‘are you going to pursue a political career in Italy?’. And that didn’t seem right.”

    The ‘wildcard’ pick

    Gezdari, who works at an investment advisory firm, has been a Tory campaigner in south west London for years. Party members are in the midst of voting for their London mayor candidate. She argues that she is not so much of an “underdog” as a “wildcard” pick. While she describes Cleverly and Akinbusoye “beautiful personalities”, she would put leader-centric politics aside, instead looking to build trust with voters and back Kemi Badenoch’s “greater good”. 

    During a half-hour conversation, Gezdari is strikingly more critical of Sir Sadiq Khan than her peers. She blames Khan for taking the “best side” of the gig by appearing on red carpets and posing beside celebrities, but for failing to “feel accountable for his failures”. She lists his stance on grooming gangs, the recent unlawful speeding fines and opposition to Palantir’s contract with the Metropolitan Police as examples of his leadership failures. 

    Then there is wasteful spending. The night tsar, Amy Lamé, who served between 2016 and 2024, was “absolutely useless” and his appointment of several deputy mayors has been “irresponsible”. Gezdari is also prepared to argue that the pedestrianisation of Oxford Street was the wrong priority at a time when several of London’s bridges are in need of repair and some are closed. 

    Gezdari wants Hammersmith Bridge back open

    In clips online, Gezdari has hit out at the £144m cost of making Oxford Street traffic-free, and directly linked it to the £300m cost of repairing Hammersmith Bridge. Khan has suggested that funding for Hammersmith Bridge is a matter for local councils. While the heavy bill for Oxford Street’s pedestrianisation has faced intense scrutiny, the plan is set to be paid for mainly through borrowing and using commercial income and events to get returns. It may be difficult for Hammersmith Bridge’s repair to be financed in the same way as Oxford Street. Nevertheless, Gezdari, who says she is “pro-finance”, raises the prospect of using sponsors on the bridge and private investment around local land to get the key crossing open to motorists again. A problem like Hammersmith Bridge is why the London mayor has to be a “champion for new business ideas”. 

    The next London mayor is set to have access to more cash than any of their predecessors. Andy Burnham’s devolution drive will allow local leaders to retain a greater portion of income taxes generated locally, as well as receipts from business rates.     Khan has already said he would use new powers to extend the Bakerloo Line. While Gezdari backs the project, she refrained from linking tax powers to public investment. She said she would support using any business tax income to offer firms relief on business rates and she ruled out introducing an overnight stay levy in London to increase investment in infrastructure. The matter of income tax receipt retention was a “bit more tricky”, adding that she would wait for further details to be revealed.

    One infrastructure project that Khan has strongly opposed is Heathrow Airport’s third runway on net zero grounds.     “I think I am very uncomfortable with Heathrow. I need to see what the new plans look like, I haven’t been talking to them and I know that there is a third runway that will go ahead now, [where] they will try and reduce the acoustic pollution and environmental impact on that,” she said, before adding that planning and parliamentary process would mean the expansion would not be delivered for some time yet. 

    “You need a mayor who has got very strong guardrails on what’s going to happen next.”

    But Gezdari is relishing the opportunity to even be considered as a possible candidate. “It’s the best thing that could have ever happened to me,” she said.
